---
title: "Solutions to Selected Exercises"
---

This appendix collects complete solutions to the starred ($\star$) exercises of every chapter. A starred
exercise is one whose statement carries the marker $\star$; its full worked solution appears here.
Solutions are organized by chapter in book order, and each is headed by the slug of the exercise it solves
together with a plain-language title, so that "Solution to @exr-lr-gm-weighted" can be located both from the
cross-reference in the chapter and from the title in this appendix. Results are cited by their slugs, for
example @thm-ols-blue or @eq-fstat, and the notation is that of [Notation](/notation.qmd).

**How to use these solutions.** These are worked derivations, not just final answers, and they are most
useful as a learning companion rather than a first port of call. The intended workflow is: attempt the
exercise yourself first; if you are stuck on the opening move, read only the **Strategy** line that begins
the harder solutions, which names the main idea or theorem without giving the algebra away, then try again;
and only afterward read the full derivation to check every step. Reading a solution before attempting the
exercise trades a small short-term gain for a large loss in understanding, because the hardest part of most
of these problems is choosing the first move, and that is exactly the skill the exercises build.

**Reading aids.** To lower the barrier for a reader who does not have the chapter open alongside, the harder
solutions carry three optional scaffolds. A **Strategy** line states the single idea that unlocks the
problem. A **Uses** line lists, in plain language, the one or two prior results the solution leans on, so
that a slug such as @thm-courant-fischer is paired with a spoken name. Scattered **Common mistake** notes
flag the conceptual confusions that recur across the book (positivity versus zero probability,
non-collapsibility versus effect modification, collapsibility versus transportability, naive versus sandwich
variance, latent versus observed correlation). None of these scaffolds is load-bearing for the mathematics;
a fluent reader can skip them, and a beginner can lean on them.

**Coverage.** Every chapter from 1 through 30 contributes at least one starred exercise, and every starred
exercise in the book has its full solution here. If you reach a starred exercise in a chapter and cannot
find its solution in this appendix, that is a defect to report; the appendix is meant to be complete for the
current book structure.

## Chapter 1: Linear Algebra I

### Solution to @exr-la1-dim-sum: The dimension formula for a sum of two subspaces

This exercise from Chapter 1 asks for the inclusion-exclusion identity
$\dim(U+W)=\dim U+\dim W-\dim(U\cap W)$.

**Strategy.** Build one basis of $U+W$ by starting from a basis of the overlap $U\cap W$ and extending it
two ways, once into $U$ and once into $W$. Counting the basis vectors then gives the formula directly; the
only real work is checking that the combined list is linearly independent.

**Uses.** The basis-extension lemma (@lem-basis-extension: any independent set extends to a basis) and the
fact that a spanning independent set is a basis.

Let $k=\dim(U\cap W)$ and choose a basis $\{\mathbf u_1,\dots,\mathbf u_k\}$ of $U\cap W$. By the
basis-extension lemma (@lem-basis-extension) extend it to a basis
$\{\mathbf u_1,\dots,\mathbf u_k,\mathbf a_1,\dots,\mathbf a_m\}$ of $U$, so $\dim U=k+m$, and separately
to a basis $\{\mathbf u_1,\dots,\mathbf u_k,\mathbf b_1,\dots,\mathbf b_n\}$ of $W$, so $\dim W=k+n$. We
claim
$$
\mathcal B=\{\mathbf u_1,\dots,\mathbf u_k,\ \mathbf a_1,\dots,\mathbf a_m,\ \mathbf b_1,\dots,\mathbf b_n\}
$$
is a basis of $U+W$.

*Spanning.* Every element of $U+W$ is $\mathbf u+\mathbf w$ with $\mathbf u\in U$ and $\mathbf w\in W$.
Writing $\mathbf u$ in the $U$-basis and $\mathbf w$ in the $W$-basis exhibits $\mathbf u+\mathbf w$ as a
combination of $\mathcal B$, so $\mathcal B$ spans $U+W$.

*Independence.* Suppose
$$
\sum_{i=1}^k \alpha_i\mathbf u_i+\sum_{r=1}^m \beta_r\mathbf a_r+\sum_{s=1}^n \gamma_s\mathbf b_s=\mathbf 0 .
$$
The idea is to isolate the part of this relation that lives only in the $W$-basis, so that we can pin it
down inside the overlap $U\cap W$ and then invoke $W$-basis independence. Accordingly, set
$\mathbf z=\sum_s \gamma_s\mathbf b_s$ (the $\mathbf b$-only piece). The displayed equation gives
$\mathbf z=-\sum_i\alpha_i\mathbf u_i-\sum_r\beta_r\mathbf a_r\in U$, while $\mathbf z\in W$ by
construction, so $\mathbf z\in U\cap W$. Thus $\mathbf z=\sum_i\delta_i\mathbf u_i$ for scalars $\delta_i$,
and $\sum_s\gamma_s\mathbf b_s-\sum_i\delta_i\mathbf u_i=\mathbf 0$. Since
$\{\mathbf u_1,\dots,\mathbf u_k,\mathbf b_1,\dots,\mathbf b_n\}$ is a basis of $W$ and hence linearly
independent, every $\gamma_s=0$ (and every $\delta_i=0$). The original relation then reads
$\sum_i\alpha_i\mathbf u_i+\sum_r\beta_r\mathbf a_r=\mathbf 0$, and the independence of the $U$-basis
forces every $\alpha_i=0$ and $\beta_r=0$. Hence $\mathcal B$ is independent.

Therefore $\dim(U+W)=k+m+n=(k+m)+(k+n)-k=\dim U+\dim W-\dim(U\cap W)$. $\square$

### Solution to @exr-la1-gram-rank: When the Gram matrix is invertible

This Chapter 1 exercise establishes when the Gram matrix $\mathbf X^\top\mathbf X$ is invertible, the linear
algebra behind the very first step of least squares.

**Uses.** The rank-nullity theorem (@thm-rank-nullity) and the definiteness of the Euclidean norm
($\|\mathbf v\|_2=0$ only for $\mathbf v=\mathbf 0$).

**(a)** If $\mathbf X\mathbf v=\mathbf 0$ then $\mathbf X^\top\mathbf X\mathbf v=\mathbf X^\top\mathbf 0=
\mathbf 0$, so $\mathcal N(\mathbf X)\subseteq\mathcal N(\mathbf X^\top\mathbf X)$. Conversely, if
$\mathbf X^\top\mathbf X\mathbf v=\mathbf 0$, then
$$
0=\mathbf v^\top\mathbf X^\top\mathbf X\mathbf v=(\mathbf X\mathbf v)^\top(\mathbf X\mathbf v)=\|\mathbf X\mathbf v\|_2^2,
$$
and the definiteness of the Euclidean norm gives $\mathbf X\mathbf v=\mathbf 0$, that is
$\mathbf v\in\mathcal N(\mathbf X)$. Hence $\mathcal N(\mathbf X^\top\mathbf X)=\mathcal N(\mathbf X)$.

**(b)** Both $\mathbf X$ and the $p\times p$ matrix $\mathbf X^\top\mathbf X$ have $p$ columns, so the
rank-nullity theorem (@thm-rank-nullity) gives
$$
\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf X^\top\mathbf X)=p-\dim\mathcal N(\mathbf X^\top\mathbf X)
=p-\dim\mathcal N(\mathbf X)=\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf X),
$$
using part (a) for the middle equality. A $p\times p$ matrix is invertible if and only if its rank is $p$,
so $\mathbf X^\top\mathbf X$ is invertible if and only if $\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf X)=p$, that is, if
and only if $\mathbf X$ has full column rank.

Why a health researcher should care: full column rank is exactly the condition that lets you estimate a
treatment effect uniquely. If two columns of $\mathbf X$ are collinear (say a covariate and a near-duplicate
of it), the rank drops below $p$, $\mathbf X^\top\mathbf X$ is singular, and infinitely many coefficient
vectors $\boldsymbol\beta$ fit the data equally well. The estimated drug effect is then not identified from
the data alone; only a modeling choice picks one value. This is the algebraic root of the collinearity
warnings that recur when a regression adjustment is used inside an indirect comparison.

**(c)** The normal equations $\mathbf X^\top\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta=\mathbf X^\top\mathbf y$ form a square
linear system with coefficient matrix $\mathbf X^\top\mathbf X$. A square system has a unique solution for
every right-hand side if and only if its matrix is invertible, which by (b) happens exactly when
$\mathbf X$ has full column rank $p$. This is the algebraic condition under which ordinary least squares
has a unique solution (@thm-ols-normal-equations). $\square$

## Chapter 2: Linear Algebra II

### Solution to @exr-parallelogram: The parallelogram law and the polarization identity

This Chapter 2 exercise proves that a norm comes from an inner product only if it obeys the parallelogram
law, and that when it does, the inner product is recovered from the norm by polarization.

**Uses.** Bilinearity of an inner product, and the definition $\|\mathbf x\|^2=\langle\mathbf x,\mathbf x\rangle$.

Let $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ be the inner product inducing $\|\mathbf x\|^2=\langle\mathbf x,\mathbf x\rangle$.
Expanding bilinearly,
$$
\begin{aligned}
\|\mathbf u+\mathbf v\|^2&=\|\mathbf u\|^2+2\langle\mathbf u,\mathbf v\rangle+\|\mathbf v\|^2,\\
\|\mathbf u-\mathbf v\|^2&=\|\mathbf u\|^2-2\langle\mathbf u,\mathbf v\rangle+\|\mathbf v\|^2 .
\end{aligned}
$$
Adding the two lines, the cross terms cancel and give the **parallelogram law**
$\|\mathbf u+\mathbf v\|^2+\|\mathbf u-\mathbf v\|^2=2\|\mathbf u\|^2+2\|\mathbf v\|^2$. Subtracting the
second line from the first gives
$\|\mathbf u+\mathbf v\|^2-\|\mathbf u-\mathbf v\|^2=4\langle\mathbf u,\mathbf v\rangle$, which is the
**polarization identity**
$\langle\mathbf u,\mathbf v\rangle=\tfrac14(\|\mathbf u+\mathbf v\|^2-\|\mathbf u-\mathbf v\|^2)$.

*Uniqueness.* Polarization writes the inner product as an explicit function of the norm alone. Hence two
inner products that induce the same norm have the same value on every pair $(\mathbf u,\mathbf v)$, so the
inner product is uniquely determined by its norm.

*The $\ell^1$ norm.* If $\|\cdot\|_1$ on $\mathbb R^2$ came from an inner product it would satisfy the
parallelogram law. Take $\mathbf u=(1,0)$, $\mathbf v=(0,1)$. Then $\|\mathbf u\|_1=\|\mathbf v\|_1=1$,
while $\mathbf u+\mathbf v=(1,1)$ and $\mathbf u-\mathbf v=(1,-1)$ both have $\ell^1$ norm $2$. The law
would require $2^2+2^2=2\cdot 1^2+2\cdot 1^2$, that is $8=4$, which is false. So $\|\cdot\|_1$ violates the
parallelogram law and cannot arise from any inner product. $\square$

### Solution to @exr-oblique-vs-orthogonal: Four equivalent characterizations of an orthogonal projection

This Chapter 2 exercise shows that four properties of an idempotent matrix $P$ (a matrix with $P^2=P$,
that is, a projection) are equivalent. Because a projection splits space into "what it keeps" (its range
$\mathcal C(P)$) and "what it kills" (its null space $\mathcal N(P)$), the four properties are four ways to
say "the split is at right angles."

**Strategy.** Prove the equivalences as a short cycle of implications rather than all pairs. The one clever
step is (iii) $\Rightarrow$ (i): to turn the size inequality $\|P\mathbf v\|\le\|\mathbf v\|$ into an
orthogonality statement, probe it with a one-parameter family of test vectors and read off the sign of an
inner product as the parameter changes sign.

**Uses.** The projection theorem (@thm-projection-theorem) and the Pythagorean identity for orthogonal
vectors.

Here are the four properties and the plain-language meaning of each, followed by the roadmap of implications
we prove.

| Label | Property | In words |
|---|---|---|
| (i) | $P=P^\top$ | the projection matrix is symmetric |
| (ii) | $P$ is the orthogonal projection onto $\mathcal C(P)$ | it drops each vector straight down onto the range |
| (iii) | $\|P\mathbf v\|\le\|\mathbf v\|$ for all $\mathbf v$ | projecting never lengthens a vector |
| (iv) | $\mathcal C(P)\perp\mathcal N(P)$ | range and null space meet at right angles |

We prove the cycle (i) $\Rightarrow$ (ii) $\Rightarrow$ (iv) $\Rightarrow$ (i), which makes (i), (ii), (iv)
equivalent, and separately (ii) $\Leftrightarrow$ (iii), which folds (iii) into the same equivalence class.

Throughout, $P^2=P$. For any idempotent, $\mathbb R^n=\mathcal C(P)\oplus\mathcal N(P)$ (a direct sum: every
vector splits uniquely as a range part plus a null-space part): indeed
$\mathbf v=P\mathbf v+(\mathbf v-P\mathbf v)$ with $P\mathbf v\in\mathcal C(P)$ and
$P(\mathbf v-P\mathbf v)=P\mathbf v-P^2\mathbf v=\mathbf 0$, so $\mathbf v-P\mathbf v\in\mathcal N(P)$;
and if $\mathbf w\in\mathcal C(P)\cap\mathcal N(P)$ then $\mathbf w=P\mathbf u$ for some $\mathbf u$ gives
$\mathbf w=P\mathbf u=P^2\mathbf u=P\mathbf w=\mathbf 0$. On $\mathcal C(P)$, $P$ acts as the identity
($P(P\mathbf u)=P\mathbf u$).

We prove (i) $\Rightarrow$ (ii) $\Rightarrow$ (iv) $\Rightarrow$ (i) and (ii) $\Leftrightarrow$ (iii).

*(i) $\Rightarrow$ (ii).* If $P=P^\top$ and $P^2=P$, then for $\mathbf m=P\mathbf u\in\mathcal C(P)$ and
$\mathbf w\in\mathcal N(P)$,
$\langle\mathbf m,\mathbf w\rangle=\langle P\mathbf u,\mathbf w\rangle=\langle\mathbf u,P^\top\mathbf w\rangle
=\langle\mathbf u,P\mathbf w\rangle=0$, so $\mathcal C(P)\perp\mathcal N(P)$. Combined with the direct-sum
decomposition, $P$ is the projection onto $\mathcal C(P)$ along its orthogonal complement, that is the
orthogonal projection onto $\mathcal C(P)$ (@thm-projection-theorem).

*(ii) $\Rightarrow$ (iv).* The orthogonal projection onto a subspace $\mathcal M$ has range $\mathcal M$
and kernel $\mathcal M^\perp$, so $\mathcal C(P)=\mathcal M\perp\mathcal M^\perp=\mathcal N(P)$.

*(iv) $\Rightarrow$ (i).* Suppose $\mathcal C(P)\perp\mathcal N(P)$. Decompose any $\mathbf x,\mathbf y$ as
$\mathbf x=\mathbf m_x+\mathbf w_x$, $\mathbf y=\mathbf m_y+\mathbf w_y$ with $\mathbf m\in\mathcal C(P)$,
$\mathbf w\in\mathcal N(P)$. Then $P\mathbf x=\mathbf m_x$, $P\mathbf y=\mathbf m_y$, and by orthogonality
$\langle P\mathbf x,\mathbf y\rangle=\langle\mathbf m_x,\mathbf m_y+\mathbf w_y\rangle
=\langle\mathbf m_x,\mathbf m_y\rangle=\langle\mathbf m_x+\mathbf w_x,\mathbf m_y\rangle
=\langle\mathbf x,P\mathbf y\rangle$. Hence $P=P^\top$.

*(ii) $\Rightarrow$ (iii).* For the orthogonal projection, decompose $\mathbf v=\mathbf m+\mathbf w$ with
$\mathbf m\perp\mathbf w$; then $\|P\mathbf v\|^2=\|\mathbf m\|^2\le\|\mathbf m\|^2+\|\mathbf w\|^2=
\|\mathbf v\|^2$ by the Pythagorean theorem, so $\|P\mathbf v\|\le\|\mathbf v\|$.

*(iii) $\Rightarrow$ (i).* Assume $\|P\mathbf v\|\le\|\mathbf v\|$ for all $\mathbf v$ and use the direct
sum $\mathbb R^n=\mathcal C(P)\oplus\mathcal N(P)$. We want to force $\langle\mathbf m,\mathbf w\rangle=0$
for a range vector $\mathbf m$ and a null-space vector $\mathbf w$. The trick is to feed the inequality a
test vector that keeps $P\mathbf v$ fixed while sliding $\mathbf v$ along the null-space direction, so that
the inequality becomes a statement about a single scalar $t$; the vector $\mathbf v=\mathbf m+t\mathbf w$
does exactly this, because $P$ annihilates $\mathbf w$ and so $P\mathbf v=\mathbf m$ for every $t$. Fix then
$\mathbf m\in\mathcal C(P)$ and $\mathbf w\in\mathcal N(P)$ and test on $\mathbf v=\mathbf m+t\mathbf w$.
Since $P\mathbf v=\mathbf m$, the contraction
inequality $\|\mathbf m\|^2\le\|\mathbf m+t\mathbf w\|^2=\|\mathbf m\|^2+2t\langle\mathbf m,\mathbf w\rangle
+t^2\|\mathbf w\|^2$ gives $0\le 2t\langle\mathbf m,\mathbf w\rangle+t^2\|\mathbf w\|^2$ for every
$t\in\mathbb R$. For small $t$ the quadratic term $t^2\|\mathbf w\|^2$ is negligible next to the linear term
$2t\langle\mathbf m,\mathbf w\rangle$, so the sign of the right-hand side is controlled by the sign of
$t\langle\mathbf m,\mathbf w\rangle$; forcing it to stay nonnegative from both sides of $t=0$ squeezes the
inner product to zero. Concretely, dividing by $t>0$ and letting $t\downarrow 0$ forces
$\langle\mathbf m,\mathbf w\rangle\ge 0$; dividing by $t<0$ (which flips the inequality) and letting
$t\uparrow 0$ forces $\langle\mathbf m,\mathbf w\rangle\le 0$. Hence $\langle\mathbf m,\mathbf w\rangle=0$
for all such $\mathbf m,\mathbf w$, that is $\mathcal C(P)\perp\mathcal N(P)$, which is (iv) and therefore
(i). This closes the cycle, so (i) through (iv) are equivalent. $\square$

Why this matters for the rest of the book: the hat matrix $H=\mathbf X(\mathbf X^\top\mathbf X)^{-1}\mathbf
X^\top$ of Chapter 6 is exactly such a symmetric idempotent, so this equivalence is what guarantees that
the least-squares fitted values $H\mathbf y$ are the orthogonal (perpendicular) drop of $\mathbf y$ onto the
column space, and hence that the residuals $\mathbf y-H\mathbf y$ are orthogonal to every fitted value. That
perpendicularity is the geometric content of the normal equations and, later, of the projection view of
covariate adjustment: a matching or standardization weight that is not a genuine orthogonal projection can
lengthen instead of shrink, which is one way an adjustment can inflate rather than reduce error.

## Chapter 3: Linear Algebra III

### Solution to @exr-ata-aat-spectrum: $A^\top A$ and $AA^\top$ share their nonzero spectrum

This Chapter 3 exercise shows that the two Gram matrices $A^\top A$ and $AA^\top$, though generally of
different sizes, carry exactly the same nonzero eigenvalues, and deduces that the singular values of $A$ and
$A^\top$ agree.

**Strategy.** The multiplication-by-$A$ map $\mathbf v\mapsto A\mathbf v$ carries an eigenvector of
$A^\top A$ to an eigenvector of $AA^\top$ for the same eigenvalue; showing this map and its mirror
$\mathbf u\mapsto A^\top\mathbf u$ are both injective gives matching eigenspace dimensions.

**Uses.** The spectral theorem (@thm-spectral-theorem), in particular that the trace equals the sum of
eigenvalues.

Let $\lambda\neq 0$ be an eigenvalue of $A^\top A$ with eigenvector $\mathbf v\neq\mathbf 0$, so
$A^\top A\mathbf v=\lambda\mathbf v$. Apply $A$:
$$
(AA^\top)(A\mathbf v)=A(A^\top A\mathbf v)=A(\lambda\mathbf v)=\lambda(A\mathbf v).
$$
Moreover $A\mathbf v\neq\mathbf 0$, since $A\mathbf v=\mathbf 0$ would give
$A^\top A\mathbf v=\mathbf 0=\lambda\mathbf v$ and hence $\mathbf v=\mathbf 0$ (as $\lambda\neq 0$),
a contradiction. So $A\mathbf v$ is an eigenvector of $AA^\top$ for the same $\lambda$. Thus the linear map
$\mathbf v\mapsto A\mathbf v$ sends the $\lambda$-eigenspace $E_\lambda(A^\top A)$ into $E_\lambda(AA^\top)$.

This map is injective on $E_\lambda(A^\top A)$: if $A\mathbf v=\mathbf 0$ with $\mathbf v\in E_\lambda$,
the same computation gives $\mathbf v=\mathbf 0$. The reverse injection is the mirror image, and because it
is the crux of the argument it is worth writing out rather than dispatching as "by symmetry." Let
$\mathbf u\neq\mathbf 0$ satisfy $AA^\top\mathbf u=\lambda\mathbf u$. Apply $A^\top$:
$$
(A^\top A)(A^\top\mathbf u)=A^\top(AA^\top\mathbf u)=A^\top(\lambda\mathbf u)=\lambda(A^\top\mathbf u),
$$
so $A^\top\mathbf u\in E_\lambda(A^\top A)$; and $A^\top\mathbf u\neq\mathbf 0$, since $A^\top\mathbf u
=\mathbf 0$ would give $AA^\top\mathbf u=\mathbf 0=\lambda\mathbf u$ and hence $\mathbf u=\mathbf 0$. Thus
$\mathbf u\mapsto A^\top\mathbf u$ injects $E_\lambda(AA^\top)$ into $E_\lambda(A^\top A)$. Two subspaces
each injecting linearly into the other have equal dimension, so $\mathbf v\mapsto A\mathbf v$ is an
isomorphism between them. Equal dimensions for every nonzero $\lambda$ means $A^\top A$ and $AA^\top$ have
exactly the same nonzero eigenvalues with the same multiplicities.

The singular values of $A$ are $\sigma_i=\sqrt{\lambda_i}$ for the nonzero eigenvalues $\lambda_i$ of
$A^\top A$; those of $A^\top$ are the square roots of the nonzero eigenvalues of $(A^\top)^\top A^\top
=AA^\top$. Since these eigenvalue lists coincide, the nonzero singular values of $A$ and of $A^\top$
coincide. Finally, $\|A\|_F^2=\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}^2=\operatorname{tr}(A^\top A)=\sum_i\lambda_i(A^\top A)
=\sum_i\sigma_i^2$, the trace being the sum of eigenvalues (@thm-spectral-theorem).

**A concrete instance.** Take the $2\times 3$ matrix $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\0&2&0\end{pmatrix}$. Then
$A^\top A=\operatorname{diag}(1,4,0)$ is $3\times 3$ with eigenvalues $\{1,4,0\}$, while
$AA^\top=\operatorname{diag}(1,4)$ is $2\times 2$ with eigenvalues $\{1,4\}$: the two share the nonzero
spectrum $\{1,4\}$, differing only in the extra zero that the larger matrix must carry. The injection
$\mathbf v\mapsto A\mathbf v$ is visible here, for the eigenvector $\mathbf v=(0,1,0)^\top$ of $A^\top A$
at $\lambda=4$ maps to $A\mathbf v=(0,2)^\top$, an eigenvector of $AA^\top$ at the same $\lambda=4$. The
singular values are $\sigma_1=\sqrt4=2$ and $\sigma_2=\sqrt1=1$, and indeed
$\|A\|_F^2=1^2+2^2=5=\sigma_1^2+\sigma_2^2$. $\square$

### Solution to @exr-weyl-inequality: Weyl's eigenvalue perturbation bounds

This Chapter 3 exercise proves Weyl's inequalities, which sandwich each eigenvalue of a sum $A+B$ between
the corresponding eigenvalue of $A$ shifted by the smallest and the largest eigenvalue of $B$.

**Strategy.** Everything comes from the variational (min-max) description of an eigenvalue as an optimized
Rayleigh quotient. Once eigenvalues are written that way, the eigenvalues of a sum inherit the additivity of
the quotient, and the lower bound is the upper bound applied to a cleverly chosen second pair.

**Uses.** The Courant-Fischer min-max theorem (@thm-courant-fischer): for a symmetric $M$, the $k$-th
smallest eigenvalue is
$$
\lambda_k(M)=\min_{\dim S=k}\ \max_{\mathbf 0\neq\mathbf x\in S}R_M(\mathbf x),
\qquad R_M(\mathbf x)=\frac{\mathbf x^\top M\mathbf x}{\mathbf x^\top\mathbf x}.
$$
Read this in words: to find $\lambda_k$, look at every $k$-dimensional subspace $S$, record the largest
Rayleigh quotient attainable inside $S$, and then take the smallest such record over all choices of $S$.
The min-max form is the only fact about eigenvalues we need.

The Rayleigh quotient is additive, $R_{A+B}(\mathbf x)=R_A(\mathbf x)+R_B(\mathbf x)$, simply because the
numerator splits: $\mathbf x^\top(A+B)\mathbf x=\mathbf x^\top A\mathbf x+\mathbf x^\top B\mathbf x$, and the
two pieces are divided by the same $\mathbf x^\top\mathbf x$. This additivity is what lets a bound on $A$
and a bound on $B$ combine into a bound on $A+B$.

*Upper bound.* Let $S^\star$ be a $k$-dimensional subspace attaining $\lambda_k(A)$, so
$\max_{\mathbf x\in S^\star}R_A(\mathbf x)=\lambda_k(A)$. For every $\mathbf x\neq\mathbf 0$,
$R_B(\mathbf x)\le\lambda_n(B)$ (the largest eigenvalue is the maximum Rayleigh quotient). Hence
$$
\lambda_k(A+B)\le\max_{\mathbf x\in S^\star}R_{A+B}(\mathbf x)
=\max_{\mathbf x\in S^\star}\bigl(R_A(\mathbf x)+R_B(\mathbf x)\bigr)
\le\lambda_k(A)+\lambda_n(B),
$$
the first inequality because $\lambda_k(A+B)$ is the minimum over all $k$-dimensional subspaces and
$S^\star$ is one of them.

*Lower bound.* The idea is that a lower bound on $\lambda_k(A+B)$ is the same as an upper bound read from
the opposite direction: recover $A$ from $A+B$ by adding $-B$, then apply the upper bound we just proved to
the pair $(A+B)$ and $(-B)$. Using $\lambda_n(-B)=-\lambda_1(B)$ (negating a symmetric matrix reverses and
sign-flips its spectrum, so the largest eigenvalue of $-B$ is minus the smallest of $B$),
$\lambda_k(A)=\lambda_k((A+B)+(-B))\le\lambda_k(A+B)+\lambda_n(-B)=\lambda_k(A+B)-\lambda_1(B)$, that is
$\lambda_k(A+B)\ge\lambda_k(A)+\lambda_1(B)$. Together,
$$
\lambda_k(A)+\lambda_1(B)\le\lambda_k(A+B)\le\lambda_k(A)+\lambda_n(B).
$$

*Consequences.* If $B\succeq 0$ then $\lambda_1(B)\ge 0$, so the lower bound gives
$\lambda_k(A+B)\ge\lambda_k(A)$ for every $k$: adding a positive semidefinite matrix cannot decrease any
eigenvalue. In general, $\lambda_1(B)\ge-\|B\|_2$ and $\lambda_n(B)\le\|B\|_2$ (the spectral norm of a
symmetric matrix is $\max_i|\lambda_i(B)|$), so the two bounds give
$-\|B\|_2\le\lambda_k(A+B)-\lambda_k(A)\le\|B\|_2$, that is
$|\lambda_k(A+B)-\lambda_k(A)|\le\|B\|_2$ for every $k$.

**A numerical check.** Let $A=\operatorname{diag}(1,3)$, so $\lambda_1(A)=1,\lambda_2(A)=3$, and perturb by
$B=\begin{pmatrix}0&0.1\\0.1&0\end{pmatrix}$, whose eigenvalues are $\pm 0.1$, so $\|B\|_2=0.1$. Then
$A+B=\begin{pmatrix}1&0.1\\0.1&3\end{pmatrix}$ has eigenvalues $\tfrac12(4\pm\sqrt{4.04})=0.99501$ and
$3.00499$. Each moved by $0.00499$ from the unperturbed value, comfortably inside the guaranteed band
$|\Delta\lambda|\le\|B\|_2=0.1$; and the two-sided Weyl bounds
$\lambda_1(A)+\lambda_1(B)=0.9\le 0.99501\le 1.1=\lambda_1(A)+\lambda_2(B)$ hold as promised.

Why this matters later: this is the statement that eigenvalues are stable, they move by no more than the
size of the perturbation. A covariance matrix estimated from data is the true covariance plus a small
error matrix $B$; Weyl's bound guarantees that its eigenvalues (hence its condition number and its
positive-definiteness) cannot jump under that error. That stability underlies the robust and sandwich
variance arguments of Chapter 5, where inverses of estimated information matrices must stay well-behaved,
and the whitening steps of weighted least squares, which require the working covariance to stay positive
definite under estimation noise. $\square$

## Chapter 4: Probability and Distributions

### Solution to @exr-cov-psd-construction: Building a normal vector with a prescribed covariance

This Chapter 4 exercise constructs a bivariate normal vector with a given correlation $\rho$ by taking the
symmetric square root of the target covariance matrix, and reads off when the construction degenerates.

**Uses.** The spectral theorem (@thm-spectral-theorem) to form $\boldsymbol\Sigma^{1/2}$, and the rule that
a linear image $\mathbf X=B\mathbf Z$ of a standard normal has covariance $BB^\top$ (@thm-cov-psd).

Write $\boldsymbol\Sigma=\begin{pmatrix}1&\rho\\\rho&1\end{pmatrix}$ with $\rho\in(-1,1)$. Its
eigenvalues solve $\det(\boldsymbol\Sigma-\lambda I)=(1-\lambda)^2-\rho^2=0$, giving
$\lambda_{\pm}=1\pm\rho$ with orthonormal eigenvectors
$\mathbf q_{+}=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(1,1)^\top$ and $\mathbf q_{-}=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(1,-1)^\top$. The spectral
decomposition (@thm-spectral-theorem) is $\boldsymbol\Sigma=Q\Lambda Q^\top$ with
$Q=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}$ and $\Lambda=\operatorname{diag}(1+\rho,1-\rho)$.
Taking nonnegative square roots of the eigenvalues,
$$
\boldsymbol\Sigma^{1/2}=Q\Lambda^{1/2}Q^\top
=\frac12\begin{pmatrix}\sqrt{1+\rho}+\sqrt{1-\rho}&\sqrt{1+\rho}-\sqrt{1-\rho}\\[2pt]
\sqrt{1+\rho}-\sqrt{1-\rho}&\sqrt{1+\rho}+\sqrt{1-\rho}\end{pmatrix},
$$
which is symmetric positive semidefinite and satisfies $\boldsymbol\Sigma^{1/2}\boldsymbol\Sigma^{1/2}
=\boldsymbol\Sigma$. Let $\mathbf Z\sim\mathcal N_2(\mathbf 0,I_2)$ and set
$\mathbf X=\boldsymbol\Sigma^{1/2}\mathbf Z$. By @thm-cov-psd (linear images of a standard normal),
$\mathbb E[\mathbf X]=\mathbf 0$ and
$\operatorname{Cov}(\mathbf X)=\boldsymbol\Sigma^{1/2}I_2\boldsymbol\Sigma^{1/2}=\boldsymbol\Sigma$, so
$\mathbf X$ has the required covariance.

The matrix fails to be positive definite exactly when an eigenvalue vanishes, that is $1+\rho=0$ or
$1-\rho=0$, that is $\rho=\pm 1$ (excluded from the open interval; the boundary is the degenerate case).
At $\rho=1$ the eigenvalue $1-\rho=0$ has eigenvector $\mathbf q_{-}=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}(1,-1)^\top$. The
factor $2$ that appears here is worth spelling out, since it comes from the length of the difference vector,
not from anywhere mysterious. Write $X_1-X_2=(1,-1)\mathbf X$; since $(1,-1)=\sqrt2\,\mathbf q_{-}^\top$
(the raw contrast is $\sqrt2$ times the unit eigenvector), we have $X_1-X_2=\sqrt2\,\mathbf q_{-}^\top\mathbf X$,
and therefore
$$
\operatorname{Var}(X_1-X_2)=(\sqrt2)^2\,\mathbf q_{-}^\top\boldsymbol\Sigma\,\mathbf q_{-}
=2\,\mathbf q_{-}^\top\boldsymbol\Sigma\,\mathbf q_{-}=2\,(1-\rho),
$$
using $\boldsymbol\Sigma\mathbf q_{-}=(1-\rho)\mathbf q_{-}$ and $\mathbf q_{-}^\top\mathbf q_{-}=1$. At
$\rho=1$ this is $2(1-1)=0$, so $X_1=X_2$ almost surely and the distribution concentrates on a line. For $\rho\in(-1,1)$ both eigenvalues are positive,
$\boldsymbol\Sigma\succ 0$, and the pair is genuinely two-dimensional. When $\rho=0$ the covariance is
$I_2$ and the two coordinates are uncorrelated; for jointly normal variables this forces independence
(@lem-normal-uncorrelated-independent), consistent with the conditional law $X_1\mid X_2$ of
@thm-mvn-conditional having mean $\rho X_2=0$ and variance $1-\rho^2=1$, free of $X_2$. $\square$

### Solution to @exr-graphoid-counterexample: The intersection axiom fails without positivity

This Chapter 4 exercise asks for a distribution that satisfies the two premises of the graphoid
intersection axiom yet violates its conclusion, showing that the axiom needs a positivity hypothesis.

**Uses.** The intersection axiom (G5) of @thm-graphoid-axioms, restated here so it can be checked without
turning back: for a probability law that is everywhere positive,
$$
\bigl(X\perp Y\mid Z,W\bigr)\ \text{and}\ \bigl(X\perp W\mid Z,Y\bigr)
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad X\perp (Y,W)\mid Z .
$$
Here *positivity* means every configuration carries strictly positive probability, $p(x,y,z,w)>0$ for every
combination of values in the supports; it is exactly this hypothesis we will violate.

**Strategy.** Make three of the variables perfect copies of a single random bit, so that conditioning on any
one of them freezes the others and both pairwise premises hold trivially, while the unconditioned trio stays
perfectly dependent, breaking the conclusion. The variable held out in the conclusion, $Z$, must be
degenerate, so that conditioning on it supplies no information and cannot itself freeze $X$.

**The construction.** Let $U\sim\mathrm{Ber}(1/2)$ and set $X=Y=W=U$ (all three equal to the same bit),
with $Z\equiv 0$ a constant. The joint law of $(X,Y,W,Z)$ puts mass $1/2$ on $(0,0,0,0)$ and mass $1/2$ on
$(1,1,1,0)$.

*The two premises hold.* Condition on $(Z,W)=(0,w)$. Given $W=w$, both $X=w$ and $Y=w$ are frozen to the
same constant, and two constants are independent, so $X\perp Y\mid(Z,W)$. Symmetrically, condition on
$(Z,Y)=(0,y)$: given $Y=y$, both $X=y$ and $W=y$ are frozen, so $X\perp W\mid(Z,Y)$. Each premise conditions
on a variable that ties down $X$, which is why it holds.

*The conclusion fails.* The conclusion of (G5) would be $X\perp(Y,W)\mid Z$. But $Z\equiv 0$ carries no
information, so this is just $X\perp(Y,W)$ unconditionally. It is false: $X$, $Y$, $W$ are the same bit, so
$P(X=1,(Y,W)=(1,1))=\tfrac12$, whereas $P(X=1)\,P((Y,W)=(1,1))=\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac12=\tfrac14$. Knowing
$(Y,W)$ determines $X$ exactly, so $X\not\perp(Y,W)\mid Z$. The conclusion of the intersection axiom is
violated even though both premises hold.

*Which step of a positivity proof breaks.* The standard proof of intersection multiplies and divides
conditional densities, using the two premises in the form
$$
p(x\mid y,z,w)=p(x\mid z,w)\quad\text{and}\quad p(x\mid y,z,w)=p(x\mid y,z),
$$
to conclude $p(x\mid z,w)=p(x\mid y,z)$ and then, letting $y$ and $w$ range freely, that this common value
depends on neither, which is the desired joint independence. Letting $y$ and $w$ range freely requires every
combination $(y,z,w)$ to have positive probability, so that each conditional density is defined. Here
positivity fails: the pair $(Y,W)$ is supported only on $(0,0)$ and $(1,1)$, so a cross-combination such as
$\{Y=1,W=0\}$ has probability zero and $p(x\mid y=1,z,w=0)$ is undefined. The substitution chain that would
propagate independence across all $(y,w)$ therefore cannot be carried out, and the deterministic tie among
$X,Y,W$ slips through the two pairwise premises undetected. $\square$

**Common mistake (positivity versus zero probability).** The tempting but wrong reading is that the
intersection axiom is an unconditional law of probability. It is not: two conditional-independence facts do
not combine into a joint one unless every relevant cell has positive mass. The same gap appears
substantively in causal inference as the positivity (overlap) assumption of Chapters 9 and 10, where a
covariate stratum that receives one treatment with probability zero blocks identification exactly as the
zero-probability cell blocks the proof here. Zero probability is not a harmless edge case to wave away; it is
precisely where deterministic ties hide.

## Chapter 5: Statistical Inference

### Solution to @exr-information-equality-fail: A nonregular model where the score identity breaks

This Chapter 5 exercise exhibits a model, the uniform on $(0,\theta)$, whose moving support violates the
regularity conditions, so the mean-zero-score identity and asymptotic normality both fail.

**Strategy.** Everything hinges on one fact: the support $(0,\theta)$ depends on the parameter, so
differentiating under the integral sign is illegal and drops a boundary term. Trace that single defect
through the score, the estimator, and its limit law.

**Uses.** The mean-zero-score identity @lem-score-mean-zero and the asymptotic-normality theorem
@thm-mle-asymptotic-normality, both of which assume the regular-model conditions of @def-regular-model.

Let $X_1,\dots,X_n$ be independent $\mathrm{Uniform}(0,\theta)$, with density $f(x;\theta)=\theta^{-1}
\mathbf 1\{0<x<\theta\}$.

**(a)** On the support, $\log f(x;\theta)=-\log\theta$, so the naive score is
$\partial_\theta\log f=-1/\theta$, a nonzero constant. Its expectation is $-1/\theta\neq 0$, so the
score-mean-zero identity @lem-score-mean-zero fails. The reason is that the interchange of differentiation
and integration underlying that identity requires a $\theta$-independent support; here the support
$(0,\theta)$ moves with $\theta$. Making this explicit with the Leibniz rule for a variable upper limit,
$\dfrac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm d\theta}\displaystyle\int_{0}^{b(\theta)}f(x,\theta)\,\mathrm dx
=f(b(\theta),\theta)\,b'(\theta)+\displaystyle\int_{0}^{b(\theta)}\partial_\theta f(x,\theta)\,\mathrm dx$,
applied to $\int_0^\theta\theta^{-1}\,\mathrm dx=1$ with $b(\theta)=\theta$ and $f=\theta^{-1}$, gives
$$
0=\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm d\theta}\!\int_0^\theta\theta^{-1}\,\mathrm dx
=\underbrace{\theta^{-1}\cdot 1}_{\text{boundary term}}
+\underbrace{\int_0^\theta(-\theta^{-2})\,\mathrm dx}_{=\,-\theta^{-1}} .
$$
The naive score $\partial_\theta\log f=-\theta^{-1}$ captures only the second, inside-the-integral piece; it
omits the boundary term $+\theta^{-1}$ contributed by the moving upper limit. That is exactly why
$\mathbb E[\text{naive score}]=-\theta^{-1}$ instead of zero: the two pieces should cancel, but the naive
score keeps only one of them.

**(b)** The likelihood is $L(\theta)=\theta^{-n}\mathbf 1\{\theta\ge\max_i X_i\}$, which is decreasing in
$\theta$ on $[\max_i X_i,\infty)$ and zero below $\max_i X_i$. It is therefore maximized at the smallest
admissible value, $\hat\theta_n=\max_i X_i=:X_{(n)}$. For $0<t<1$,
$$
P\bigl(X_{(n)}\le t\theta\bigr)=\prod_{i=1}^n P(X_i\le t\theta)=t^n,
$$
so $P\bigl(n(\theta-X_{(n)})/\theta>s\bigr)=P\bigl(X_{(n)}<\theta(1-s/n)\bigr)=(1-s/n)^n\to e^{-s}$ for
each $s>0$. Hence $n(\theta-\hat\theta_n)/\theta\xrightarrow{d}\mathrm{Exp}(1)$. The estimation error is of
order $1/n$, not $1/\sqrt n$, and the limit law is exponential, not normal.

**(c)** The asymptotic-normality theorem @thm-mle-asymptotic-normality assumes a regular model
(@def-regular-model): in particular a common support independent of $\theta$, twice differentiability of
the log-likelihood in a neighborhood of the truth, and a finite positive Fisher information obtained by
differentiating under the integral. Every one of these fails here. The support depends on $\theta$ (so
@def-regular-model is violated and @lem-score-mean-zero does not hold), the maximizer sits on the boundary
rather than at an interior stationary point of a smooth log-likelihood (assumption A1 fails), and there is
no quadratic expansion of the log-likelihood about the truth driving a $\sqrt n$ central limit theorem. The
faster $n$-rate and the non-normal exponential limit are the signature of this nonregular, boundary
problem. $\square$

### Solution to @exr-sandwich-derivation: Sandwich versus model-based variance under overdispersion

This Chapter 5 exercise fits a mean by a deliberately wrong (Poisson) working model and shows that the
sandwich variance, unlike the naive model-based variance, stays correct when the data are overdispersed.

**Strategy.** Treat the Poisson score as an estimating function, not a true likelihood. The M-estimation
sandwich then supplies the honest variance, and comparing it to the model-based variance isolates a single
inflation factor.

**Uses.** The M-estimation sandwich variance @def-sandwich-variance (bread
$\mathbf A=-\mathbb E[\partial_\mu\psi]$, meat $\mathbf B=\mathbb E[\psi^2]$).

Two pieces of vocabulary first, since the whole solution turns on them. A *working* model is a model we fit
on purpose even though we do not believe it, using its score as an estimating equation vehicle; here the
"working Poisson" is used only to define an estimator of the mean, and we make no claim that the counts are
truly Poisson. And we write $\kappa$ for the *overdispersion ratio*, the index of dispersion
$\kappa=\operatorname{Var}(X)/\mathbb E[X]=v_0/\mu_0$, the true variance-to-mean ratio; $\kappa=1$ is the
Poisson case, and $\kappa>1$ is overdispersion (more scatter than Poisson allows). Throughout,
$\mu_0=\mathbb E[X]$ and $v_0=\operatorname{Var}(X)$, so $v_0=\kappa\mu_0$.

The working Poisson log-likelihood contribution is $x\log\mu-\mu$.

**(a)** Differentiating in $\mu$ gives the working score
$\psi(x;\mu)=\partial_\mu(x\log\mu-\mu)=x/\mu-1$. The estimating equation
$\sum_i\psi(X_i;\mu)=0$ reads $\sum_i(X_i/\mu-1)=0$, that is $\mu=\bar X_n$, so the M-estimator is
$\hat\mu_n=\bar X_n$. Its target $\mu^\star$ solves the population equation $\mathbb E[\psi(X;\mu^\star)]=0$,
that is $\mathbb E[X]/\mu^\star-1=0$, so $\mu^\star=\mathbb E[X]=\mu_0$: the working estimator is consistent
for the true mean even though the variance is misspecified.

**(b)** Using the M-estimation sandwich of @def-sandwich-variance with bread
$\mathbf A(\mu)=-\mathbb E[\partial_\mu\psi(X;\mu)]$ and meat $\mathbf B(\mu)=\mathbb E[\psi(X;\mu)^2]$,
evaluated at $\mu_0$:
$$
\mathbf A(\mu_0)=-\mathbb E\!\left[-\frac{X}{\mu_0^2}\right]=\frac{\mathbb E[X]}{\mu_0^2}=\frac{\mu_0}{\mu_0^2}=\frac{1}{\mu_0},
$$
$$
\mathbf B(\mu_0)=\mathbb E\!\left[\Bigl(\frac{X}{\mu_0}-1\Bigr)^2\right]=\frac{\operatorname{Var}(X)}{\mu_0^2}
=\frac{v_0}{\mu_0^2}=\frac{\kappa\mu_0}{\mu_0^2}=\frac{\kappa}{\mu_0}.
$$
The sandwich asymptotic variance is
$$
\frac1n\,\mathbf A(\mu_0)^{-1}\mathbf B(\mu_0)\mathbf A(\mu_0)^{-1}
=\frac1n\,\mu_0\cdot\frac{\kappa}{\mu_0}\cdot\mu_0=\frac{\kappa\,\mu_0}{n}.
$$
The naive model-based variance assumes correct Poisson specification, under which the variance equals the
inverse information $\mathbf A(\mu_0)^{-1}/n=\mu_0/n$.

**(c)** The ratio of sandwich to naive variance is $\kappa$, so the naive standard error
$\sqrt{\mu_0/n}$ understates the true standard error $\sqrt{\kappa\mu_0/n}$ by the factor $\sqrt\kappa>1$.
This is exactly the situation of @cor-sandwich-collapse read in reverse: when the model is correct
($\kappa=1$), bread and meat agree, $\mathbf A=\mathbf B=1/\mu_0=\mathcal I$, and the sandwich collapses to
the inverse-information variance $\mu_0/n$; overdispersion ($\kappa>1$) drives meat above bread and inflates
the true variance by $\kappa$, which only the sandwich estimator captures. $\square$

## Chapter 6: Linear Regression from First Principles

### Solution to @exr-lr-gm-weighted: The weighted (generalized) Gauss-Markov theorem

This Chapter 6 exercise extends the Gauss-Markov optimality of ordinary least squares to correlated,
unequal-variance errors, showing that generalized (weighted) least squares is the best linear unbiased
estimator.

**Strategy.** Do not re-run the whole optimality proof. Instead *whiten* the model by multiplying through
by $V^{-1/2}$, which turns the correlated errors into spherical ones, apply the ordinary Gauss-Markov
theorem to the whitened model, and translate the conclusion back.

**Uses.** The ordinary Gauss-Markov theorem @thm-ols-blue and the symmetric square root $V^{-1/2}$ from the
spectral theorem @thm-spectral-theorem.

Replace G2 by $\operatorname{Cov}(\boldsymbol\varepsilon)=\sigma^2 V$ with $V\succ 0$ known, and define
$\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}_V=(\mathbf X^\top V^{-1}\mathbf X)^{-1}\mathbf X^\top V^{-1}\mathbf y$.

*Unbiasedness and covariance.* With $\mathbb E[\mathbf y]=\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta$,
$$
\mathbb E[\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}_V]=(\mathbf X^\top V^{-1}\mathbf X)^{-1}\mathbf X^\top V^{-1}\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta
=\boldsymbol\beta,
$$
so $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}_V$ is unbiased. Writing $G=(\mathbf X^\top V^{-1}\mathbf X)^{-1}\mathbf X^\top V^{-1}$,
$$
\operatorname{Cov}(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}_V)=G\,(\sigma^2 V)\,G^\top
=\sigma^2(\mathbf X^\top V^{-1}\mathbf X)^{-1}\mathbf X^\top V^{-1}\,V\,V^{-1}\mathbf X(\mathbf X^\top V^{-1}\mathbf X)^{-1}
=\sigma^2(\mathbf X^\top V^{-1}\mathbf X)^{-1}.
$$

*Optimality (generalized Gauss-Markov).* Factor $V^{-1}=W^\top W$ with $W$ invertible (the symmetric square
root $V^{-1/2}$ from the spectral theorem @thm-spectral-theorem serves, with $W=W^\top=V^{-1/2}$). Apply
$W$ to the model: set $\tilde{\mathbf y}=W\mathbf y$, $\tilde{\mathbf X}=W\mathbf X$,
$\tilde{\boldsymbol\varepsilon}=W\boldsymbol\varepsilon$. Then
$\tilde{\mathbf y}=\tilde{\mathbf X}\boldsymbol\beta+\tilde{\boldsymbol\varepsilon}$ with
$\mathbb E[\tilde{\boldsymbol\varepsilon}]=\mathbf 0$ and
$\operatorname{Cov}(\tilde{\boldsymbol\varepsilon})=W(\sigma^2 V)W^\top=\sigma^2 W V W^\top
=\sigma^2 (W V^{1/2})(W V^{1/2})^\top$. Since $W=V^{-1/2}$, $WVW^\top=V^{-1/2}VV^{-1/2}=I$, so the
transformed model satisfies the ordinary Gauss-Markov hypotheses G1, G2, G3 with spherical errors of
variance $\sigma^2 I$. The ordinary least squares estimator in the transformed model is
$$
(\tilde{\mathbf X}^\top\tilde{\mathbf X})^{-1}\tilde{\mathbf X}^\top\tilde{\mathbf y}
=(\mathbf X^\top W^\top W\mathbf X)^{-1}\mathbf X^\top W^\top W\mathbf y
=(\mathbf X^\top V^{-1}\mathbf X)^{-1}\mathbf X^\top V^{-1}\mathbf y=\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}_V,
$$
so $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}_V$ is exactly the OLS estimator of the whitened model. By the ordinary
Gauss-Markov theorem (@thm-ols-blue) it is the best linear unbiased estimator there. Linear unbiased
estimators of $\boldsymbol\beta$ in the original model correspond bijectively to linear unbiased estimators
in the transformed model (the bijection $\mathbf y\mapsto W\mathbf y$ is invertible and carries one class
onto the other), and the estimand and the variance are unchanged by the relabeling. Hence
$\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}_V$ is the best linear unbiased estimator under $\operatorname{Cov}(\boldsymbol
\varepsilon)=\sigma^2V$, generalizing @thm-ols-blue.

The optimality holds only because $V$ is the true error covariance. The matching-adjusted estimator of
Chapter 18 also reweights patients, but its weights are chosen to balance covariates against a target
population, not to invert an error covariance. Under homoskedastic errors such weights raise the variance
above that of ordinary least squares; MAIC accepts this cost in order to change the estimand to the target
population, and Chapter 18 measures the cost through the effective sample size. $\square$

### Solution to @exr-lr-general-hypothesis: General linear hypothesis equals the nested-model $F$ test

This Chapter 6 exercise proves that the Wald-style statistic for a general linear hypothesis
$R\boldsymbol\beta=\mathbf q$ is algebraically identical to the extra-sum-of-squares $F$ statistic from
comparing the constrained and unconstrained fits.

**Strategy.** Solve the constrained least-squares problem with a Lagrange multiplier, express the residual
sum of squares gap as a single quadratic form in the constraint discrepancy $R\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}-\mathbf q$,
and match it term for term against the $F$ statistic.

**Uses.** The normal equations $\mathbf X^\top(\mathbf y-\mathbf X\hat{\boldsymbol\beta})=\mathbf 0$ and the
sampling theory of @thm-general-linear-hypothesis.

Let the full model have least-squares fit $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$ with residual sum of squares
$\mathrm{RSS}_1=S(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta})$, where $S(\mathbf b)=\|\mathbf y-\mathbf X\mathbf b\|^2$. The
reduced model is the constrained fit minimizing $S$ over the affine set $\{\mathbf b:R\mathbf b=\mathbf q\}$;
call its minimizer $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}_R$ and its residual sum of squares
$\mathrm{RSS}_0=S(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}_R)$. We show the general-linear-hypothesis statistic @eq-glh-stat
equals the nested-model statistic @eq-fstat with $q=\operatorname{rank}(R)$ degrees of freedom in the
numerator.

*Constrained minimization.* Minimize $S(\mathbf b)$ subject to $R\mathbf b=\mathbf q$ with a Lagrange
multiplier $\boldsymbol\lambda\in\mathbb R^q$. Stationarity of
$S(\mathbf b)+2\boldsymbol\lambda^\top(R\mathbf b-\mathbf q)$ gives
$-2\mathbf X^\top(\mathbf y-\mathbf X\mathbf b)+2R^\top\boldsymbol\lambda=\mathbf 0$, that is
$\mathbf X^\top\mathbf X\mathbf b=\mathbf X^\top\mathbf y-R^\top\boldsymbol\lambda$. Since
$\mathbf X^\top\mathbf X\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}=\mathbf X^\top\mathbf y$,
$$
\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}_R=\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}-(\mathbf X^\top\mathbf X)^{-1}R^\top\boldsymbol\lambda .
$$
Impose the constraint $R\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}_R=\mathbf q$:
$R\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}-R(\mathbf X^\top\mathbf X)^{-1}R^\top\boldsymbol\lambda=\mathbf q$, so with
$A=R(\mathbf X^\top\mathbf X)^{-1}R^\top$ (positive definite, hence invertible, as in
@thm-general-linear-hypothesis),
$$
\boldsymbol\lambda=A^{-1}(R\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}-\mathbf q).
$$

*Difference of residual sums of squares.* Let
$\mathbf d=\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}_R-\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}=-(\mathbf X^\top\mathbf X)^{-1}R^\top\boldsymbol
\lambda$, and write $\mathbf r=\mathbf y-\mathbf X\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$ for the unconstrained residual, so
$\mathrm{RSS}_1=\|\mathbf r\|^2$. Evaluate $S$ at $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}_R=\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}+\mathbf d$
by expanding the squared norm:
$$
S(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}+\mathbf d)=\|\mathbf y-\mathbf X(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}+\mathbf d)\|^2
=\|\mathbf r-\mathbf X\mathbf d\|^2
=\|\mathbf r\|^2-2\,\mathbf d^\top\mathbf X^\top\mathbf r+\mathbf d^\top\mathbf X^\top\mathbf X\mathbf d .
$$
The middle term vanishes because $\mathbf X^\top\mathbf r=\mathbf X^\top(\mathbf y-\mathbf X\hat{\boldsymbol
\beta})=\mathbf 0$ by the normal equations, so $S(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}+\mathbf d)=\|\mathbf r\|^2
+\mathbf d^\top\mathbf X^\top\mathbf X\mathbf d$ and hence
$$
\mathrm{RSS}_0-\mathrm{RSS}_1=S(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}_R)-S(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta})
=\mathbf d^\top\mathbf X^\top\mathbf X\mathbf d .
$$
Substituting $\mathbf d$,
$$
\mathbf d^\top\mathbf X^\top\mathbf X\mathbf d
=\boldsymbol\lambda^\top R(\mathbf X^\top\mathbf X)^{-1}\mathbf X^\top\mathbf X(\mathbf X^\top\mathbf X)^{-1}R^\top\boldsymbol\lambda
=\boldsymbol\lambda^\top A\boldsymbol\lambda
=(R\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}-\mathbf q)^\top A^{-1}(R\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}-\mathbf q),
$$
using $\boldsymbol\lambda=A^{-1}(R\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}-\mathbf q)$ and $A^\top=A$.

*Equality of the statistics.* The constrained model adds $q=\operatorname{rank}(R)$ restrictions, so it has
$p_0=p-q$ free parameters and the nested-model statistic @eq-fstat is
$$
F=\frac{(\mathrm{RSS}_0-\mathrm{RSS}_1)/q}{\mathrm{RSS}_1/(n-p)}
=\frac{(R\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}-\mathbf q)^\top A^{-1}(R\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}-\mathbf q)/q}{s^2},
$$
where $s^2=\mathrm{RSS}_1/(n-p)$. This is exactly @eq-glh-stat. Both statistics therefore coincide as random
variables; in particular the sampling distribution $F_{q,n-p}$ established for @eq-glh-stat in
@thm-general-linear-hypothesis (via the whitening identity that $\mathbf v\sim\mathcal N_q(\mathbf 0,
\sigma^2A)$ implies $\mathbf v^\top A^{-1}\mathbf v/\sigma^2\sim\chi^2_q$) is the distribution of the
nested-model $F$ as well. $\square$

## Chapter 7: Generalized Linear Models

### Solution to @exr-glm-irls-probit: IRLS for the probit link, and why Fisher scoring differs from Newton

This Chapter 7 exercise derives the iteratively reweighted least squares (IRLS) weights and working response
for the probit link, then explains why, because probit is a non-canonical link, Fisher scoring and
Newton-Raphson are genuinely different algorithms.

**Strategy.** The IRLS pieces come straight from the general GLM formulas by plugging in the probit mean and
variance. The subtle part is the last: differentiate the score once more and watch a residual-weighted term
survive in the observed information but average to zero in the expected information.

**Uses.** The GLM information weight @eq-glm-information, the working response @eq-working-response, and the
canonical-link Hessian lemma @lem-canonical-hessian.

For the probit link $g(\mu)=\Phi^{-1}(\mu)$, the mean is $\mu=g^{-1}(\eta)=\Phi(\eta)$, so
$\mathrm d\mu/\mathrm d\eta=\Phi'(\eta)$ and $g'(\mu)=\mathrm d\eta/\mathrm d\mu=1/\Phi'(\eta)$, where
$\Phi'=\phi$ is the standard normal density.

*Working weights.* For binomial data with denominator $n_i$ the variance of the proportion is
$\operatorname{Var}(Y_i)=\mu_i(1-\mu_i)/n_i=\Phi(\eta_i)(1-\Phi(\eta_i))/n_i$. The GLM information weight
of @eq-glm-information is $W_i=(\mathrm d\mu_i/\mathrm d\eta_i)^2/\operatorname{Var}(Y_i)$, hence
$$
W_i=\frac{\Phi'(\eta_i)^2}{\Phi(\eta_i)(1-\Phi(\eta_i))/n_i}
=\frac{n_i\,\Phi'(\eta_i)^2}{\Phi(\eta_i)\bigl(1-\Phi(\eta_i)\bigr)},
$$
the stated formula.

*Working response.* By @eq-working-response,
$z_i=\eta_i+(y_i-\mu_i)g'(\mu_i)=\eta_i+\dfrac{y_i-\Phi(\eta_i)}{\Phi'(\eta_i)}$. Each IRLS step
(@thm-irls) solves the weighted normal equations $\mathbf X^\top\mathbf W\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta
=\mathbf X^\top\mathbf W\mathbf z$ with these $W_i$ and $z_i$, evaluated at the current iterate.

*Observed versus expected information.* This is the conceptual punchline, so we write the Hessian out. For a
canonical link the Hessian of the log-likelihood is nonstochastic, so the observed Hessian equals its
expectation and Fisher scoring coincides with Newton-Raphson (@lem-canonical-hessian). The probit link is
non-canonical, and the difference surfaces on differentiating the score once more. Write $c(\eta)$ for the
coefficient factor
$$
c(\eta)=\frac{\mathrm d\mu/\mathrm d\eta}{\operatorname{Var}(Y)}=\frac{\phi(\eta)}{\Phi(\eta)\bigl(1-\Phi(\eta)\bigr)}
$$
(taking $n_i=1$ for transparency), so the score is
$\mathbf U(\boldsymbol\beta)=\sum_i(y_i-\mu_i)\,c(\eta_i)\,\mathbf x_i$. Differentiating in
$\boldsymbol\beta$, with $\eta_i=\mathbf x_i^\top\boldsymbol\beta$ and $\mathrm d\mu_i/\mathrm d\eta_i=\phi(\eta_i)$,
the product rule gives
$$
\nabla^2\ell=\sum_i\Bigl[(y_i-\mu_i)\,c'(\eta_i)-c(\eta_i)\,\phi(\eta_i)\Bigr]\mathbf x_i\mathbf x_i^\top .
$$
The observed information $-\nabla^2\ell$ keeps the data-residual term $(y_i-\mu_i)\,c'(\eta_i)$; the expected
information replaces $y_i-\mu_i$ by its mean $0$, dropping that term and leaving
$\sum_i c(\eta_i)\phi(\eta_i)\mathbf x_i\mathbf x_i^\top=\sum_i\phi(\eta_i)^2/[\Phi(\eta_i)(1-\Phi(\eta_i))]\,\mathbf x_i\mathbf x_i^\top
=\mathbf X^\top\mathbf W\mathbf X$, the Fisher-scoring weight matrix. So the two informations differ by
exactly $\sum_i(y_i-\mu_i)\,c'(\eta_i)\,\mathbf x_i\mathbf x_i^\top$, and everything comes down to whether
$c'(\eta)$ vanishes. It does not, in general: using $\phi'(\eta)=-\eta\phi(\eta)$ and
$\tfrac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm d\eta}[\Phi(1-\Phi)]=\phi(1-2\Phi)$, the quotient rule gives
$$
c'(\eta)=\frac{\phi(\eta)\bigl[-\eta\,\Phi(\eta)(1-\Phi(\eta))-\phi(\eta)(1-2\Phi(\eta))\bigr]}{\bigl[\Phi(\eta)(1-\Phi(\eta))\bigr]^2},
$$
which is not identically zero; it is nonzero for every $\eta\neq 0$, vanishing only at the isolated point
$\eta=0$ where the two bracketed terms cancel. Because the residual term therefore does not drop out,
observed and expected information differ, and Fisher scoring (which uses the expected information
$\mathbf X^\top\mathbf W\mathbf X$) is not identical to Newton-Raphson, in contrast to the canonical case,
where $c'\equiv 0$ makes the residual term disappear. $\square$

### Solution to @exr-glm-noncollapse: The odds ratio is non-collapsible and attenuates toward the null

This Chapter 7 exercise proves that marginalizing a constant conditional odds ratio over a covariate strictly
shrinks it toward $1$, so the marginal odds ratio lies between the null and the conditional value. This is
non-collapsibility, and it is the reason odds ratios do not transport across populations with different
covariate mixes.

**Strategy.** Rewrite each marginal odds as a single scalar function $A(a)$ of the odds-multiplier $a$
(equal to $1$ for control, $\omega$ for treatment), and prove two monotonicity facts about $A$: it
increases (giving $\omega^{\mathrm M}>1$) but grows sub-linearly, $A(a)/a$ decreasing (giving
$\omega^{\mathrm M}<\omega$).

**Uses.** The covariance inequality for like-monotone functions (two functions that both increase in the
same variable have nonnegative covariance).

**Common mistake (non-collapsibility versus effect modification).** The attenuation proved here happens
*even when the conditional odds ratio $\omega$ is identical in every stratum*, that is, with no effect
modification at all. Non-collapsibility is a property of the nonlinear odds scale, not evidence that the
treatment works differently in different subgroups. Do not read a marginal-conditional gap as effect
modification; a constant conditional odds ratio still produces a population-dependent marginal one.

Let $X\in\{0,1\}$ with $P(X=1)=\pi$, constant conditional odds ratio $\omega>1$ on the logit scale, and
baseline risks $\mu_0(0)\neq\mu_0(1)$. Under the no-confounding identity of @sec-noncollapsibility,
$\mathbb E[Y(t)]=\mathbb E_X[\mu_t(X)]$, the marginal odds ratio is
$\omega^{\mathrm M}=\dfrac{\mathbb E[\mu_1(X)]/(1-\mathbb E[\mu_1(X)])}{\mathbb E[\mu_0(X)]/(1-\mathbb E[\mu_0(X)])}$.

**(a) A numerical example.** Take $\pi=\tfrac12$ and baseline risks $\mu_0(0)=0.1$, $\mu_0(1)=0.5$, with
$\omega=4$. Solving $\mu_1(x)/(1-\mu_1(x))=4\,\mu_0(x)/(1-\mu_0(x))$ gives the treated risks
$\mu_1(0)=\dfrac{4(1/9)}{1+4(1/9)}=\dfrac{4/9}{13/9}=\tfrac{4}{13}=0.30769$ and
$\mu_1(1)=\dfrac{4(1)}{1+4(1)}=\tfrac45=0.8$. The marginal risks are
$\mathbb E[\mu_0]=\tfrac12(0.1+0.5)=0.3$ and $\mathbb E[\mu_1]=\tfrac12(0.30769+0.8)=0.55385$, so
$$
\omega^{\mathrm M}=\frac{0.55385/0.44615}{0.3/0.7}=\frac{1.24138}{0.42857}=2.8966,
$$
which lies strictly between $1$ and $\omega=4$. The conditional log odds ratio $\log 4=1.3863$ is
attenuated to the marginal $\log 2.8966=1.0635$.

To make the attenuation visible as the covariate prevalence $\pi=P(X=1)$ moves, hold the conditional risks
(and hence the conditional odds ratio $\omega=4$) fixed and recompute the marginal odds ratio at several
prevalences:

| $\pi=P(X=1)$ | $\mathbb E[\mu_0]$ | $\mathbb E[\mu_1]$ | marginal OR $\omega^{\mathrm M}$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| $0.00$ | $0.100$ | $0.30769$ | $4.0000$ |
| $0.25$ | $0.200$ | $0.43077$ | $3.0270$ |
| $0.50$ | $0.300$ | $0.55385$ | $2.8966$ |
| $0.75$ | $0.400$ | $0.67692$ | $3.1429$ |
| $1.00$ | $0.500$ | $0.80000$ | $4.0000$ |

The marginal odds ratio equals the conditional value $4$ only at the two degenerate endpoints ($\pi=0$ or
$\pi=1$, where the covariate carries no variation), and dips below it in between, reaching its strongest
attenuation near $\pi=0.5$ where the baseline-odds spread is largest. Non-collapsibility is therefore a
distributional effect: the same two treatments carry a different marginal odds ratio in every population,
with no change in any conditional parameter.

**(b) The general bound.** Write the baseline odds as the random variable
$W=\mu_0(X)/(1-\mu_0(X))$, which is non-degenerate because $\mu_0(0)\neq\mu_0(1)$. The constant-odds-ratio
relation gives $\mu_0(X)=W/(1+W)$ and $\mu_1(X)=\omega W/(1+\omega W)$. The right object to introduce is the
marginal odds that result when every stratum's baseline odds $W$ is multiplied by a common factor $a$. Under
that tilt the stratum risk becomes $aW/(1+aW)$, so the marginal odds (marginal risk over one minus marginal
risk) is the ratio below. For $a>0$ set
$$
A(a)=\frac{\mathbb E[aW/(1+aW)]}{\mathbb E[1/(1+aW)]},
\qquad\text{so}\qquad
\frac{\mathbb E[\mu_0]}{1-\mathbb E[\mu_0]}=A(1),\quad\frac{\mathbb E[\mu_1]}{1-\mathbb E[\mu_1]}=A(\omega),
$$
using $1-aW/(1+aW)=1/(1+aW)$. In words, $A(a)$ is the marginal odds when every conditional odds is scaled by
$a$: at $a=1$ it is the control marginal odds and at $a=\omega$ the treated marginal odds, so
$\omega^{\mathrm M}=A(\omega)/A(1)$. The whole problem has now been reduced to understanding how the single
scalar function $A$ grows.

First, $A$ is strictly increasing. Writing $D(a)=\mathbb E[1/(1+aW)]$ and noting
$aW/(1+aW)=1-1/(1+aW)$, we get $A(a)=(1-D(a))/D(a)=1/D(a)-1$. The integrand $1/(1+aW)$ is strictly
decreasing in $a$ on the event $\{W>0\}$, which has probability one (risks lie in $(0,1)$), so $D$ is
strictly decreasing, $1/D$ strictly increasing, and $A$ strictly increasing. Since $\omega>1$ and
$A(1)>0$, this yields $\omega^{\mathrm M}=A(\omega)/A(1)>1$.

Second, $a\mapsto A(a)/a$ is strictly decreasing. Indeed
$A(a)/a=\mathbb E[W/(1+aW)]/\mathbb E[1/(1+aW)]=\mathbb E_{Q_a}[W]$, the mean of $W$ under the tilted law
$\mathrm dQ_a/\mathrm dP\propto 1/(1+aW)$. By the standard exponential-tilt identity,
$$
\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm da}\mathbb E_{Q_a}[W]
=\operatorname{Cov}_{Q_a}\!\Bigl(W,\ \frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm da}\log\frac{1}{1+aW}\Bigr)
=-\operatorname{Cov}_{Q_a}\!\Bigl(W,\ \frac{W}{1+aW}\Bigr)<0,
$$
because $W$ and $W/(1+aW)$ are both strictly increasing in $W$, so their covariance is positive (strictly,
since $W$ is non-degenerate). Hence $A(a)/a$ is strictly decreasing, and with $\omega>1$,
$\dfrac{\omega^{\mathrm M}}{\omega}=\dfrac{A(\omega)/\omega}{A(1)}=\dfrac{\mathbb E_{Q_\omega}[W]}{\mathbb E_{Q_1}[W]}<1$,
that is $\omega^{\mathrm M}<\omega$.

Together $1<\omega^{\mathrm M}<\omega$: the marginal odds ratio lies strictly between the null and the
conditional value, so the odds ratio is attenuated toward the null and is non-collapsible. The engine of the
argument is the covariance inequality for like-monotone functions (both $w\mapsto w$ and $w\mapsto w/(1+aw)$
increase in the baseline odds $w$). Equality $\omega^{\mathrm M}=\omega$ would require $W$ degenerate, that is equal baseline risks,
which is the agreement-iff-degenerate clause of @cor-emcoll-or-attenuation.

For a health technology assessment the message is concrete: if a trial reports a conditional (adjusted) odds
ratio and a competitor reports a marginal (unadjusted) one, the two are not on the same footing even with no
bias and no effect modification, because marginalizing over a different patient mix moves the odds ratio on
its own. An indirect comparison that mixes conditional and marginal odds ratios, or that transports a
marginal odds ratio to a population with a different covariate distribution, will be biased for this reason
alone. $\square$

## Chapter 8: Hierarchical Models, Shrinkage, and Bayesian Inference

### Solution to @exr-james-stein-sure: Stein's unbiased risk estimate and James-Stein domination

This Chapter 8 exercise derives Stein's unbiased risk estimate (SURE), uses it to show that the James-Stein
shrinkage estimator beats the raw estimator in $J\ge 3$ dimensions, and reads the result as the frequentist
justification for partial pooling in meta-analysis.

**Strategy.** SURE turns the unknowable risk into a computable expectation by trading the cross term
$\mathbb E[(\mathbf Y-\boldsymbol\theta)^\top\mathbf g]$ for a divergence $\mathbb E[\nabla\cdot\mathbf g]$
via Stein's lemma; then the specific James-Stein $\mathbf g$ makes the divergence and the squared shrinkage
combine into a single negative term.

**Uses.** Stein's lemma @lem-stein (for $Y\sim\mathcal N(\theta,\sigma^2)$,
$\mathbb E[(Y-\theta)h(Y)]=\sigma^2\mathbb E[h'(Y)]$) and the risk identity @thm-james-stein.

Let $\mathbf Y\sim\mathcal N_J(\boldsymbol\theta,\sigma^2 I_J)$ with $J\ge 3$ and
$\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}=\mathbf Y+\mathbf g(\mathbf Y)$.

**(a) Stein's unbiased risk estimate.** Expand the loss:
$$
\|\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}-\boldsymbol\theta\|^2=\|\mathbf Y-\boldsymbol\theta+\mathbf g(\mathbf Y)\|^2
=\|\mathbf Y-\boldsymbol\theta\|^2+2(\mathbf Y-\boldsymbol\theta)^\top\mathbf g(\mathbf Y)+\|\mathbf g(\mathbf Y)\|^2 .
$$
Take expectations term by term. First $\mathbb E\|\mathbf Y-\boldsymbol\theta\|^2=J\sigma^2$. For the cross
term, apply Stein's lemma (@lem-stein) coordinatewise: with $Y_j\sim\mathcal N(\theta_j,\sigma^2)$ and the
other coordinates held fixed,
$\mathbb E[(Y_j-\theta_j)g_j(\mathbf Y)]=\sigma^2\,\mathbb E[\partial g_j/\partial Y_j]$. Summing over $j$,
$\mathbb E[(\mathbf Y-\boldsymbol\theta)^\top\mathbf g(\mathbf Y)]=\sigma^2\,\mathbb E[\nabla\cdot\mathbf g(\mathbf Y)]$.
Hence
$$
\mathbb E\|\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}-\boldsymbol\theta\|^2
=\mathbb E\bigl[J\sigma^2+2\sigma^2\nabla\cdot\mathbf g(\mathbf Y)+\|\mathbf g(\mathbf Y)\|^2\bigr].
$$

**(b) The James-Stein choice.** Put $\mathbf g(\mathbf y)=-(J-2)\sigma^2\mathbf y/\|\mathbf y\|^2$. Then
$\|\mathbf g(\mathbf y)\|^2=(J-2)^2\sigma^4/\|\mathbf y\|^2$. For the divergence, differentiate the $j$-th
component $g_j(\mathbf y)=-(J-2)\sigma^2\,y_j/\|\mathbf y\|^2$ by the quotient rule, using
$\partial\|\mathbf y\|^2/\partial y_j=2y_j$:
$$
\frac{\partial}{\partial y_j}\frac{y_j}{\|\mathbf y\|^2}
=\frac{1\cdot\|\mathbf y\|^2-y_j\cdot 2y_j}{\|\mathbf y\|^4}
=\frac{\|\mathbf y\|^2-2y_j^2}{\|\mathbf y\|^4},
\qquad\text{so}\qquad
\frac{\partial g_j}{\partial y_j}=-(J-2)\sigma^2\,\frac{\|\mathbf y\|^2-2y_j^2}{\|\mathbf y\|^4}.
$$
Summing over $j=1,\dots,J$ and using $\sum_j\|\mathbf y\|^2=J\|\mathbf y\|^2$ together with
$\sum_j y_j^2=\|\mathbf y\|^2$,
$$
\nabla\cdot\mathbf g=-(J-2)\sigma^2\,\frac{\sum_j\bigl(\|\mathbf y\|^2-2y_j^2\bigr)}{\|\mathbf y\|^4}
=-(J-2)\sigma^2\,\frac{J\|\mathbf y\|^2-2\|\mathbf y\|^2}{\|\mathbf y\|^4}
=-(J-2)\sigma^2\,\frac{(J-2)\|\mathbf y\|^2}{\|\mathbf y\|^4}
=-\frac{(J-2)^2\sigma^2}{\|\mathbf y\|^2}.
$$
Substituting,
$$
\mathbb E\|\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}^{\mathrm{JS}}-\boldsymbol\theta\|^2
=J\sigma^2+2\sigma^2\Bigl(-(J-2)^2\sigma^2\,\mathbb E\tfrac{1}{\|\mathbf Y\|^2}\Bigr)
+(J-2)^2\sigma^4\,\mathbb E\tfrac{1}{\|\mathbf Y\|^2}
=J\sigma^2-(J-2)^2\sigma^4\,\mathbb E\!\left[\tfrac{1}{\|\mathbf Y\|^2}\right],
$$
which is the risk identity of @thm-james-stein, strictly below $J\sigma^2$ because the subtracted term is
positive when $J\ge 3$. The positive-part estimator
$\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}^{\mathrm{JS+}}=(1-(J-2)\sigma^2/\|\mathbf Y\|^2)_{+}\mathbf Y$ replaces the
shrinkage factor by its nonnegative part. When the raw factor $1-(J-2)\sigma^2/\|\mathbf Y\|^2$ is negative,
$\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}^{\mathrm{JS}}$ points opposite to $\mathbf Y$ and overshoots the origin, which is
never a sensible estimate; truncating the factor at $0$ replaces it by the origin on that event and leaves
it unchanged elsewhere. This truncation *dominates in risk*: the positive-part estimator has weakly smaller
risk than $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}^{\mathrm{JS}}$ for every $\boldsymbol\theta$, and strictly smaller
whenever the truncation event has positive probability. The claim is about expected loss, not realized loss:
it is not true that the truncated estimate is closer to $\boldsymbol\theta$ for every sample and every
$\boldsymbol\theta$ (for a $\boldsymbol\theta$ lying far along the $-\mathbf Y$ direction the untruncated,
sign-flipped estimate can occasionally be closer on a given draw), so the domination is a statement about
risk, the average over samples, not a pointwise-in-outcome guarantee.

**Why the threshold is $J\ge 3$.** The subtracted term $(J-2)^2\sigma^4\,\mathbb E[1/\|\mathbf Y\|^2]$
strictly improves the risk exactly when two conditions both hold: the coefficient $(J-2)^2$ is nonzero, and
the expectation $\mathbb E[1/\|\mathbf Y\|^2]$ is finite. For $J=2$ the coefficient is $(2-2)^2=0$, so
$\mathbf g\equiv\mathbf 0$ and James-Stein is just the raw estimator, with no gain. For $J=1$ the
coefficient is nonzero but $\mathbb E[1/Y^2]=\infty$ (the reciprocal of a one-degree-of-freedom chi-square
has an infinite mean), so the SURE identity is vacuous; and indeed in one or two dimensions the raw
estimator is admissible (Stein's theorem), so no shrinkage estimator of this form can dominate it. Only from
$J=3$ on are both $(J-2)^2>0$ and $\mathbb E[1/\|\mathbf Y\|^2]<\infty$, which is why "three or more" is the
exact dividing line.

**(c) Meta-analytic reading.** Treating the $J\ge 3$ study-specific effect estimates as
$\mathbf Y\sim\mathcal N_J(\boldsymbol\theta,\sigma^2 I)$, the James-Stein shrinkage pulls each study toward
a fixed center (the origin in (b), or any prespecified point after recentering) and, by (b), strictly
reduces total mean squared error relative to reporting the separate unpooled estimates. The partial pooling
of random-effects meta-analysis (Chapter 13) shrinks each study's estimate toward the *estimated* pooled
mean by an amount set by the estimated between-study variance; estimating the center spends one dimension,
and the corresponding Efron-Morris estimator, with $J-3$ in place of $J-2$, dominates the raw estimates once
there are at least four studies. Either way, such shrinkage cannot hurt and typically helps the total mean
squared error. The justification is frequentist and
prior-free: dominance holds for every $\boldsymbol\theta$, so the gain from borrowing strength across
studies does not depend on adopting any subjective prior distribution for the effects. For an evidence
synthesis this is reassurance that pooling several related estimates (treatment contrasts in a network,
subgroup effects) is not merely a Bayesian convenience but improves accuracy under the sampling distribution
alone. $\square$

### Solution to @exr-reml-one-way: REML variance components in the balanced one-way model

This Chapter 8 exercise computes the restricted maximum likelihood (REML) estimators of the within- and
between-group variances in a balanced one-way random-effects model, and shows they equal the
analysis-of-variance estimators, with the $I-1$ (not $I$) divisor that ordinary maximum likelihood misses.

**Strategy.** REML estimates variances from *error contrasts*, the part of the data that is free of the
unknown mean. In the balanced design these contrasts split cleanly into a within-group block and a
between-group block, each a scaled chi-square, so matching each mean square to its expectation solves the
problem.

**Uses.** The one-sample REML variance correction @thm-reml-one-sample and the chi-square distribution of a
sample sum of squares of independent normals.

A word on the vocabulary, since it recurs. An *error contrast* is a linear combination $\mathbf c^\top
\mathbf y$ of the data whose coefficient vector is orthogonal to the design column of the fixed effect, here
$\mathbf 1_{In}$ (the all-ones vector of length $In$, since there are $I$ groups of $n$ observations). Such
a combination has $\mathbb E[\mathbf c^\top\mathbf y]=\mu\,\mathbf c^\top\mathbf 1_{In}=0$, so its
distribution is free of the unknown grand mean $\mu$; REML forms the likelihood from a maximal set of these
mean-free combinations, which is exactly what removes the downward bias of ordinary maximum likelihood.

Consider $y_{ij}=\mu+\theta_i+\varepsilon_{ij}$, $i=1,\dots,I$, $j=1,\dots,n$, with
$\theta_i\sim\mathcal N(0,\tau^2)$, $\varepsilon_{ij}\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2)$, all independent. Let
$\bar y_{i\cdot}=\tfrac1n\sum_j y_{ij}$, $\bar y_{\cdot\cdot}=\tfrac1{In}\sum_{ij}y_{ij}$, and define the
balanced mean squares
$$
\mathrm{MS}_{\mathrm W}=\frac{1}{I(n-1)}\sum_{i,j}(y_{ij}-\bar y_{i\cdot})^2,
\qquad
\mathrm{MS}_{\mathrm B}=\frac{n}{I-1}\sum_{i}(\bar y_{i\cdot}-\bar y_{\cdot\cdot})^2 .
$$

**(a) REML estimators.** REML maximizes the likelihood of a maximal set of error contrasts, the linear
combinations orthogonal to the design column $\mathbf 1_{In}$ (which carries the only fixed effect $\mu$).
Two chi-square facts make the balanced computation explicit, and each is a short calculation rather than an
article of faith.

*Within-group block.* The within-group contrasts $y_{ij}-\bar y_{i\cdot}$ subtract off each group mean, so
the common $\mu$ and the group effect $\theta_i$ cancel and only the errors remain:
$y_{ij}-\bar y_{i\cdot}=\varepsilon_{ij}-\bar\varepsilon_{i\cdot}$. For each group $i$ these are the centered
residuals of $n$ independent $\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2)$ errors, so $\sum_j(y_{ij}-\bar y_{i\cdot})^2/\sigma^2
\sim\chi^2_{n-1}$; the $I$ groups are independent, and adding $I$ independent $\chi^2_{n-1}$ variables gives
$\sum_{i,j}(y_{ij}-\bar y_{i\cdot})^2/\sigma^2\sim\chi^2_{I(n-1)}$, that is
$I(n-1)\mathrm{MS}_{\mathrm W}/\sigma^2\sim\chi^2_{I(n-1)}$, with $\mathbb E[\mathrm{MS}_{\mathrm W}]=\sigma^2$.

*Between-group block.* The group means are $\bar y_{i\cdot}=\mu+\theta_i+\bar\varepsilon_{i\cdot}$ with
$\theta_i\sim\mathcal N(0,\tau^2)$ and $\bar\varepsilon_{i\cdot}\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2/n)$ independent, so
$\bar y_{i\cdot}\sim\mathcal N(\mu,\tau^2+\sigma^2/n)$ independently across $i$. The between-group contrasts
$\bar y_{i\cdot}-\bar y_{\cdot\cdot}$ are orthogonal to $\mathbf 1_{In}$ and to the within-group block, and
$\sum_i(\bar y_{i\cdot}-\bar y_{\cdot\cdot})^2/(\tau^2+\sigma^2/n)\sim\chi^2_{I-1}$ as the centered sum of
squares of $I$ independent normals. Since $\sum_i(\bar y_{i\cdot}-\bar y_{\cdot\cdot})^2=(I-1)\mathrm{MS}_{\mathrm B}/n$
and $n(\tau^2+\sigma^2/n)=n\tau^2+\sigma^2$, this reads
$(I-1)\mathrm{MS}_{\mathrm B}/(n\tau^2+\sigma^2)\sim\chi^2_{I-1}$ with
$\mathbb E[\mathrm{MS}_{\mathrm B}]=n\tau^2+\sigma^2$. Because these two chi-square blocks are
independent and together span the error-contrast space, the restricted log-likelihood separates and is
maximized by matching each mean square to its expectation:
$$
\hat\sigma^2_{\mathrm{REML}}=\mathrm{MS}_{\mathrm W},
\qquad
n\hat\tau^2_{\mathrm{REML}}+\hat\sigma^2_{\mathrm{REML}}=\mathrm{MS}_{\mathrm B},
\quad\text{so}\quad
\hat\tau^2_{\mathrm{REML}}=\frac{\mathrm{MS}_{\mathrm B}-\mathrm{MS}_{\mathrm W}}{n}.
$$
These are exactly the analysis-of-variance estimators.

**(b) The divisor $I-1$ versus $I$.** The between-group sum of squares is divided by $I-1$ in
$\mathrm{MS}_{\mathrm B}$ because REML works with the $I-1$ between-group contrasts orthogonal to
$\mathbf 1_{In}$, spending one degree of freedom on the estimated grand mean $\bar y_{\cdot\cdot}$
(equivalently on $\mu$). Ordinary maximum likelihood does not remove the fixed effect before estimating the
variance components; its profile treats $\mu$ as known at $\bar y_{\cdot\cdot}$ and divides the same
between-group sum of squares by $I$, giving
$\hat\tau^2_{\mathrm{ML}}=\bigl(\tfrac{I-1}{I}\mathrm{MS}_{\mathrm B}-\mathrm{MS}_{\mathrm W}\bigr)/n$, which
is biased downward. REML's $I-1$ corrects precisely for the degree of freedom consumed by estimating $\mu$,
reproducing the analysis-of-variance estimator.

**(c) Truncation.** Both estimators are truncated at zero, since a variance cannot be negative. The REML
estimate is truncated when $\mathrm{MS}_{\mathrm B}<\mathrm{MS}_{\mathrm W}$, that is when the observed
between-group spread does not exceed what the within-group noise alone would produce; then
$\hat\tau^2_{\mathrm{REML}}=0$. This is the balanced one-way instance of the truncation in the
DerSimonian-Laird estimator @eq-dersimonian-laird, where $\hat\tau^2$ is set to zero whenever the
heterogeneity statistic falls below its null expectation. $\square$

## Chapter 9: Potential Outcomes and Identification

### Solution to @exr-po-positivity-failure: Positivity failure leaves a counterfactual mean unidentified

This Chapter 9 exercise shows that when one covariate stratum receives a treatment with probability zero,
that stratum's counterfactual mean, and hence the average treatment effect, is not identified from the data
at all.

**Uses.** The adjustment (standardization) formula @eq-ate-identification and the positivity requirement of
@sec-po-bridge.

Let $X\in\{0,1\}$ with $P(X=1)=\tfrac12$, $e(0)=P(T=1\mid X=0)=0$, $e(1)=0.5$, under SUTVA and strong
ignorability.

**(a)** The adjustment formula @eq-ate-identification expresses $\mathbb E[Y(1)]$ through the observed
regression $\mathbb E[Y\mid T=1,X=x]$ averaged over $x$. In the stratum $X=0$ the conditioning event
$\{T=1,X=0\}$ has probability $P(T=1,X=0)=P(X=0)e(0)=\tfrac12\cdot 0=0$, so $\mathbb E[Y\mid T=1,X=0]$
conditions on a null event and is undefined. The treated branch of the adjustment formula therefore cannot
be evaluated: there are no treated units in stratum $X=0$ to estimate $\mu_1(0)$.

**(b)** Strong ignorability identifies $\mu_1(0)=\mathbb E[Y(1)\mid X=0]$ only through treated units in
that stratum, of which there are none. Hence the observed-data law places no constraint on $\mu_1(0)$:
two data-generating processes that agree on everything observable can differ in $\mu_1(0)$. Concretely,
keep $\mu_1(1)=\mathbb E[Y(1)\mid X=1]$, $\mu_0(0)$, $\mu_0(1)$ fixed at any values consistent with the
observed conditional means, and consider $\mu_1(0)\in\{0,10\}$. Both choices reproduce the identical
observed law (since stratum $X=0$ contributes no treated outcomes), yet
$$
\mathbb E[Y(1)]=\tfrac12\mu_1(0)+\tfrac12\mu_1(1)
$$
differs by $\tfrac12(10-0)=5$ between them, so the average treatment effect $\tau=\mathbb E[Y(1)]
-\mathbb E[Y(0)]$ is not identified. Positivity failure in one stratum leaves a whole counterfactual mean
free.

**(c)** This is the covariate-overlap requirement of @sec-po-bridge in microcosm. An indirect comparison
transports an effect from a source population to a target only on the region of covariate space where both
treatments are represented. A stratum that receives one treatment with probability zero is an extrapolation
region: the comparison there rests entirely on an uncheckable modeling assumption, exactly as $\mu_1(0)$ is
here unconstrained by data. Concretely, in a MAIC or STC (Chapters 18 and 19) suppose the individual-level
trial enrolled no patients over age 65 but the aggregate target population contains many such patients. Then
the matching weights would have to place weight where the source has no data, and the outcome regression
would have to predict outcomes for a covariate value it never saw; the reweighted or standardized comparison
in the elderly subgroup is then pure extrapolation, supported by the model's functional form rather than by
observed outcomes. Overlap of the covariate distributions is what makes the population-adjusted estimand
identifiable rather than assumption-driven, and its failure is exactly the sort of gap a weight-diagnostic
(a near-zero effective sample size) or an out-of-range covariate mean is meant to catch before an indirect
comparison is trusted. $\square$

### Solution to @exr-po-selection-bias-proof: A symmetric decomposition of naive selection bias

This Chapter 9 exercise decomposes the naive (unadjusted) difference in group means into an average
treatment effect plus a symmetric selection-bias term, and shows the bias vanishes under randomization.

**Uses.** The consistency identity @thm-consistency-identity ($\mathbb E[Y\mid T=t]=\mathbb E[Y(t)\mid T=t]$)
and the ATT-side decomposition @eq-naive-decomposition.

**Control-side decomposition.** By the consistency identity (@thm-consistency-identity), the observed group
means are potential-outcome means, $\mathbb E[Y\mid T=1]=\mathbb E[Y(1)\mid T=1]$ and
$\mathbb E[Y\mid T=0]=\mathbb E[Y(0)\mid T=0]$, so
$\Delta_{\mathrm{naive}}=\mathbb E[Y(1)\mid T=1]-\mathbb E[Y(0)\mid T=0]$. Now add and subtract the
counterfactual treated mean among the controls, $\mathbb E[Y(1)\mid T=0]$:
$$
\Delta_{\mathrm{naive}}
=\underbrace{\bigl(\mathbb E[Y(1)\mid T=0]-\mathbb E[Y(0)\mid T=0]\bigr)}_{\textstyle \tau_{\mathrm C}}
+\underbrace{\bigl(\mathbb E[Y(1)\mid T=1]-\mathbb E[Y(1)\mid T=0]\bigr)}_{\text{treated-outcome selection}} .
$$
The first bracket is $\mathbb E[Y(1)-Y(0)\mid T=0]=\tau_{\mathrm C}$, the average effect among the
controls (ATC). This is the control-side analogue of @thm-naive-selection-bias.

**The symmetric average.** Averaging this decomposition with the ATT-side decomposition
@eq-naive-decomposition,
$\Delta_{\mathrm{naive}}=\tau_{\mathrm T}+(\mathbb E[Y(0)\mid T=1]-\mathbb E[Y(0)\mid T=0])$, gives
$$
\Delta_{\mathrm{naive}}=\tfrac12(\tau_{\mathrm T}+\tau_{\mathrm C})
+\tfrac12\Bigl[\bigl(\mathbb E[Y(0)\mid T=1]-\mathbb E[Y(0)\mid T=0]\bigr)
+\bigl(\mathbb E[Y(1)\mid T=1]-\mathbb E[Y(1)\mid T=0]\bigr)\Bigr].
$$
The leading term is the average of ATT and ATC. The bracketed symmetric bias term averages two
between-group differences: the gap in the untreated potential outcome $Y(0)$ and the gap in the treated
potential outcome $Y(1)$ between those who took treatment and those who did not. It compares the two groups
on *both* potential outcomes rather than one, and so is symmetric in the roles of treatment and control.

**Vanishing under marginal ignorability.** If $(Y(0),Y(1))\perp T$, then
$\mathbb E[Y(0)\mid T=1]=\mathbb E[Y(0)\mid T=0]$ and $\mathbb E[Y(1)\mid T=1]=\mathbb E[Y(1)\mid T=0]$, so
each of the two between-group differences is zero and the symmetric bias term vanishes. Independence also
gives $\tau_{\mathrm T}=\tau_{\mathrm C}=\tau$, so $\Delta_{\mathrm{naive}}=\tfrac12(\tau+\tau)=\tau$,
recovering @cor-naive-unbiased-rct. $\square$

## Chapter 10: Adjustment Methods

### Solution to @exr-stabilized: Stabilized inverse-probability weights have mean one

This Chapter 10 exercise verifies that stabilized inverse-probability weights average to one and explains
why stabilizing lowers the variance of the weighted estimator without changing its target.

**Uses.** The propensity definition $\mathbb E[T\mid X]=e(X)$ and the worked example @exm-adjustment-worked.

Let $sw=T\,p_1/e(X)+(1-T)\,p_0/(1-e(X))$ with $p_1=P(T=1)$, $p_0=P(T=0)=1-p_1$.

**(a)** Condition on $X$ and use $\mathbb E[T\mid X]=e(X)$, $\mathbb E[1-T\mid X]=1-e(X)$:
$$
\mathbb E[sw\mid X]=\frac{p_1}{e(X)}\,\mathbb E[T\mid X]+\frac{p_0}{1-e(X)}\,\mathbb E[1-T\mid X]
=\frac{p_1}{e(X)}e(X)+\frac{p_0}{1-e(X)}(1-e(X))=p_1+p_0=1
$$
pointwise in $X$. Taking expectations, $\mathbb E[sw]=1$.

**(b)** In @exm-adjustment-worked, $e(0)=0.2$, $e(1)=0.6$, $P(X=0)=P(X=1)=\tfrac12$, and
$p_1=P(T=1)=\tfrac12(0.2)+\tfrac12(0.6)=0.4$, $p_0=0.6$. The four cell values of $sw$ are
$$
\begin{aligned}
(T=1,x=0):\ &\tfrac{0.4}{0.2}=2.0, & (T=1,x=1):\ &\tfrac{0.4}{0.6}=0.6\overline{6},\\
(T=0,x=0):\ &\tfrac{0.6}{0.8}=0.75, & (T=0,x=1):\ &\tfrac{0.6}{0.4}=1.5 .
\end{aligned}
$$
The cell probabilities are $P(T=1,x=0)=\tfrac12(0.2)=0.1$, $P(T=1,x=1)=\tfrac12(0.6)=0.3$,
$P(T=0,x=0)=\tfrac12(0.8)=0.4$, $P(T=0,x=1)=\tfrac12(0.4)=0.2$. The $P$-weighted average is
$$
0.1(2.0)+0.3(0.6\overline 6)+0.4(0.75)+0.2(1.5)=0.2+0.2+0.3+0.3=1.0,
$$
confirming $\mathbb E[sw]=1$.

**(c)** The stabilized treated weight is the raw weight $T/e(X)$ times the constant $p_1$, so
$\operatorname{Var}(T\,p_1/e(X))=p_1^2\operatorname{Var}(T/e(X))$, smaller because $p_1<1$. The Hájek
estimator divides the weighted sum of outcomes by the weighted sum of weights, so a common constant $p_1$
cancels between numerator and denominator: the estimate of $\mathbb E[Y(1)]$, and hence its variance, is
unchanged. (The Horvitz-Thompson estimator, which divides by $n$ instead, would be scaled by $p_1$ and would
need the constant divided back out.) Stabilization therefore recenters the weights at one, which makes
weight diagnostics interpretable, but improves precision only in marginal structural models whose weight
numerators are not constant. $\square$

### Solution to @exr-eif-control: Efficient influence function and efficiency bound for the control mean

This Chapter 10 exercise writes down the efficient influence function and the semiparametric efficiency
bound for the control-arm mean $\psi_0=\mathbb E[Y(0)]$, mirroring the treated-arm result, and evaluates the
bound on the worked example.

**Uses.** The treated-arm efficient influence function and bound @thm-eif-bound, mirrored by the symmetry
$T\mapsto 1-T$.

An efficiency bound is the smallest asymptotic variance any regular estimator of the target can achieve; it
