$\gamma_C=0$). The conditional $A$-versus-$B$ contrast is the SEMA constant $\gamma_A-\gamma_B$ (the
interaction cancels). Evaluating each arm's linear predictor at the two covariate values, $\eta_k(0)=\mu_{*}+\gamma_k$
and $\eta_k(1)=\mu_{*}+\boldsymbol\beta_1+\boldsymbol\beta_2+\gamma_k$.

**(b) The closed-form gap.** Rather than write one three-line formula, name the pieces. The marginal risk
under each arm is the two-point average
$$
\bar\theta_A=(1-q)\operatorname{expit}(\mu_{*}+\gamma_A)+q\operatorname{expit}(\mu_{*}+\boldsymbol\beta_1+\boldsymbol\beta_2+\gamma_A),
$$
$$
\bar\theta_B=(1-q)\operatorname{expit}(\mu_{*}+\gamma_B)+q\operatorname{expit}(\mu_{*}+\boldsymbol\beta_1+\boldsymbol\beta_2+\gamma_B),
$$
the marginal contrast is the logit difference
$\Delta_{BA}(\mathcal P^{*})=\operatorname{logit}\bar\theta_A-\operatorname{logit}\bar\theta_B$, and the
non-collapsibility gap is the conditional minus the marginal,
$$
\text{gap}=(\gamma_A-\gamma_B)-\Delta_{BA}(\mathcal P^{*})
=(\gamma_A-\gamma_B)-\bigl(\operatorname{logit}\bar\theta_A-\operatorname{logit}\bar\theta_B\bigr).
$$
Substituting $\bar\theta_A,\bar\theta_B$ gives the single closed-form expression, now assembled from four
readable ingredients rather than presented as one wall of symbols.

**(c) Degenerate cases.** If $q\in\{0,1\}$ the covariate is degenerate: at $q=0$, $\bar\theta_k=\operatorname{expit}(\mu_{*}+\gamma_k)$
and $\operatorname{logit}\bar\theta_A-\operatorname{logit}\bar\theta_B=\gamma_A-\gamma_B$, so the gap is
zero; the same holds at $q=1$. If $\boldsymbol\beta_1+\boldsymbol\beta_2=0$, the active-arm linear
predictors $\eta_A,\eta_B$ are constant in $x$ (no spread), so again $\bar\theta_k=\operatorname{expit}(\mu_{*}+\gamma_k)$
and the gap is zero. Both vanishing conditions are exactly those of @thm-aggregation-bias: a degenerate
covariate or no spread in the active-arm linear predictors leaves nothing to average over.

**(d) Numerical check.** At the inputs of @exm-mlnmr-new-target ($\mu_{*}=-0.5$, $\boldsymbol\beta_1=0.4$,
$\boldsymbol\beta_2=0.5$, $\gamma_A=0.8$, $\gamma_B=0.3$, $q=0.6$),
$\bar\theta_A=0.4\operatorname{expit}(0.3)+0.6\operatorname{expit}(1.2)=0.690892$ and
$\bar\theta_B=0.4\operatorname{expit}(-0.2)+0.6\operatorname{expit}(0.7)=0.580979$, so
$\Delta_{BA}(\mathcal P^{*})=\operatorname{logit}(0.690892)-\operatorname{logit}(0.580979)=0.804292-0.326794=0.477498$,
and the gap is $(\gamma_A-\gamma_B)-0.477498=0.5-0.477498=0.022502$, matching the chapter. SEMA cannot
eliminate the gap because it pins the conditional contrast to a constant but the marginal contrast
involves logit-of-average minus average-of-logit, the non-collapsibility (Jensen) discrepancy, which
persists whenever the covariate has spread and $q\in(0,1)$. $\square$

### Solution to @exr-mlnmr-stc-reduction: Marginal STC is a special case of ML-NMR

This Chapter 23 exercise shows that marginal STC is exactly ML-NMR restricted to fitting on the IPD alone
and fixing the target to the comparator population; the extra aggregate-data information and the free choice
of target population are what a full ML-NMR fit adds.

**Uses.** The ML-NMR aggregate arm mean @eq-mlnmr-est-aggmean, the aggregation identity @thm-aggregation, and
STC consistency @thm-stc-consistency.

Fix a logistic outcome family with linear predictor $\eta_k(\mathbf x;\boldsymbol\xi)$ and inverse link
$g^{-1}=\operatorname{expit}$. Marginal STC (Chapter 19) for an IPD trial on $\{A,C\}$ standardized to the
comparator covariate distribution $f_{BC}$ predicts the arm means
$$
\hat\mu_k^{\mathrm{STC}}=\int \operatorname{expit}\!\bigl(\eta_k(\mathbf x;\hat{\boldsymbol\xi})\bigr)\,f_{BC}(\mathbf x)\,\mathrm d\mathbf x,\qquad k\in\{A,C\},
$$
and reports $g(\hat\mu_C^{\mathrm{STC}})-g(\hat\mu_A^{\mathrm{STC}})$. The ML-NMR aggregate arm mean
@eq-mlnmr-est-aggmean over the same target $f_{BC}$ using the same fitted linear predictor is
$$
\bar\theta_{\bullet k}=\int \operatorname{expit}\!\bigl(\eta_k(\mathbf x;\hat{\boldsymbol\xi})\bigr)\,f_{BC}(\mathbf x)\,\mathrm d\mathbf x .
$$
These are the identical functional of $\hat{\boldsymbol\xi}$: both integrate $\operatorname{expit}(\eta_k)$
against $f_{BC}$ and contrast on the link scale. Hence marginal STC is ML-NMR restricted to (i) fitting the
outcome surface on the IPD alone and (ii) fixing the target population to the comparator $f_{BC}$.

Two things distinguish a full ML-NMR fit from this restriction. First, ML-NMR's likelihood incorporates the
aggregate-data *outcomes* through the aggregation identity @thm-aggregation: the AgD arm contributes its
observed event summary to the likelihood, so the fitted $\hat{\boldsymbol\xi}$ uses information that STC
(fitting on the IPD only) ignores. Second, ML-NMR's estimand @thm-target-population-integral admits any
target population, not only $f_{BC}$, so it can report the contrast standardized to a decision population
different from the comparator trial.

Therefore STC is the special case of ML-NMR obtained by fitting on the IPD alone and fixing the target to
$f_{BC}$. The extra information ML-NMR uses changes the answer when the AgD outcomes are informative about
shared parameters, for instance when the comparator arm's observed event rate sharpens the prognostic or
baseline parameters that also enter the IPD arms, shifting $\hat{\boldsymbol\xi}$ and hence the contrast. It
does not change the answer when the IPD already identifies $\boldsymbol\xi$ and the target is the comparator
population with no extrapolation, the no-extrapolation regime of Chapter 18, in which STC is consistent
(@thm-stc-consistency) and the AgD outcomes add precision but not a different limit. $\square$

## Chapter 24: Bayesian Computation and Diagnostics

### Solution to @exr-comp-rhat-floor: The algebraic floor of the potential scale reduction factor

This Chapter 24 exercise shows that the $\widehat R$ convergence diagnostic has a hard lower bound
$\sqrt{(N-1)/N}$ set by the number of iterations, is centered at $1$ at convergence, and is pushed above $1$
by autocorrelation-inflated between-chain variance.

**Uses.** The between/within variance definitions @eq-comp-wb, @eq-comp-vhat and the expectation lemmas
@lem-comp-within, @lem-comp-between.

**The algebraic floor.** From the definitions @eq-comp-wb and @eq-comp-vhat,
$\widehat V=(1-\tfrac1N)W+\tfrac1N B$, so dividing by $W>0$,
$$
\frac{\widehat V}{W}=\Bigl(1-\frac1N\Bigr)+\frac1N\frac{B}{W}=\frac{N-1}{N}+\frac{B}{NW}.
$$
Since $B\ge 0$, $\widehat V/W\ge (N-1)/N$, hence
$\widehat R=\sqrt{\widehat V/W}\ge\sqrt{(N-1)/N}$ always. This floor is a striking practical fact for short
chains: at $N=4$ draws it is $\sqrt{3/4}=0.866$, at $N=100$ draws it is $\sqrt{99/100}=0.995$, and it rises
to $1$ as $N\to\infty$. So with only four iterations per chain the diagnostic can never read below $0.866$
no matter how perfectly the chains agree; the floor reflects the estimator's construction, not convergence.
Moreover $\widehat R\ge 1$ if and only if $\widehat V/W\ge 1$, that is $(N-1)/N+B/(NW)\ge 1$, that is
$B/(NW)\ge 1/N$, that is $B\ge W$.

**Centering at convergence.** In the iid-within-chain idealization a single chain mean of $N$ independent
draws has variance $v_N=\sigma^2/N$. By @lem-comp-within,
$\mathbb E[W]=\tfrac{N}{N-1}(\sigma^2-v_N)=\tfrac{N}{N-1}\sigma^2\tfrac{N-1}{N}=\sigma^2$, and by
@lem-comp-between, $\mathbb E[B]=Nv_N=\sigma^2$. Thus $\mathbb E[B]=\mathbb E[W]=\sigma^2$, so
$\widehat V/W$ is centered at $(N-1)/N+\sigma^2/(N\sigma^2)=(N-1)/N+1/N=1$ and $\widehat R$ is centered at
$1$ at convergence.

**What pushes $\widehat R$ above $1$.** The term that lifts $\widehat R$ above one is the between-chain term
$B$, through $B/(NW)$. When the chains are positively autocorrelated but share a common stationary law, the
variance of a chain mean is inflated by the integrated autocorrelation time $\tau_{\mathrm{int}}=1+2\sum_{k\ge 1}\rho_k>1$,
namely $v_N\approx(\sigma^2/N)\tau_{\mathrm{int}}$, so $\mathbb E[B]=Nv_N\approx\sigma^2\tau_{\mathrm{int}}>\sigma^2$
while $\mathbb E[W]$ stays near $\sigma^2$. Then $\widehat V/W\approx(N-1)/N+\tau_{\mathrm{int}}/N=1+(\tau_{\mathrm{int}}-1)/N$
and $\widehat R\approx\sqrt{1+(\tau_{\mathrm{int}}-1)/N}>1$. The excess of the autocorrelation-inflated
between-chain variance over the within-chain variance, captured by $B/(NW)$, is what holds $\widehat R$
above one until the chains mix. $\square$

### Solution to @exr-comp-gpd: Generalized Pareto tail moments and the PSIS-LOO shape thresholds

This Chapter 24 exercise finds which moments of a generalized Pareto tail are finite as a function of its
shape parameter $k$, then reads those thresholds as the reliability tiers of the Pareto-smoothed importance
sampling (PSIS) leave-one-out diagnostic.

**Strategy.** A power-law tail $f(x)\sim Cx^{-1/k-1}$ has a finite $m$-th moment exactly when the integrand
$x^m f(x)$ decays fast enough to integrate at infinity; the threshold is a one-line exponent comparison.

**Uses.** The generalized Pareto moment lemma @lem-comp-gpd-moments and the PSIS reliability theorem
@thm-comp-psis-reliability. As a reminder of the vocabulary, PSIS-LOO is leave-one-out cross-validation
carried out by importance sampling: each held-out point is scored by reweighting the full-data posterior
draws with *importance ratios* $r_i$ (the ratio of the leave-one-out to the full posterior density), and the
predictive quantity is a *self-normalized importance estimator* (a weighted average with weights $r_i$
divided by their sum). PSIS stabilizes the largest of these ratios by fitting a generalized Pareto
distribution to their upper tail, whose estimated shape $\widehat k$ is the diagnostic below.

**Moments of the generalized Pareto tail.** Let $\bar F(x)=(1+kx/\sigma)^{-1/k}$ for $x\ge 0$ with $k>0$,
density $f(x)=\sigma^{-1}(1+kx/\sigma)^{-1/k-1}$. To read off the tail behavior, factor out the dominant
power inside the bracket: $1+kx/\sigma=(kx/\sigma)\bigl(1+\sigma/(kx)\bigr)$, so
$$
f(x)=\sigma^{-1}\Bigl(\tfrac{kx}{\sigma}\Bigr)^{-1/k-1}\Bigl(1+\tfrac{\sigma}{kx}\Bigr)^{-1/k-1}
\xrightarrow[x\to\infty]{}\ \sigma^{-1}\Bigl(\tfrac{k}{\sigma}\Bigr)^{-1/k-1}x^{-1/k-1}=C\,x^{-1/k-1},
$$
since $(1+\sigma/(kx))^{-1/k-1}\to 1$, with $C=\sigma^{-1}(k/\sigma)^{-1/k-1}>0$. Hence
$x^m f(x)\sim C x^{m-1/k-1}$. The tail integral $\int^{\infty}x^{m-1/k-1}\,\mathrm dx$
converges if and only if the exponent is below $-1$, that is $m-1/k-1<-1$, that is $m<1/k$. Hence
$\mathbb E[X^m]<\infty$ if and only if $m<1/k$ (@lem-comp-gpd-moments). Setting $m=1$ gives a finite mean
iff $k<1$; setting $m=2$ gives a finite variance iff $k<1/2$.

**Relation to PSIS-LOO reliability.** The importance ratios $r_i$ in PSIS-LOO have a generalized Pareto
upper tail with estimated shape $\widehat k_i$. By the moment thresholds: if $\widehat k_i<\tfrac12$ the
ratios have finite variance, so the self-normalized importance estimator obeys a $\sqrt S$ central limit
theorem and the estimate is reliable; if $\tfrac12\le\widehat k_i<1$ the mean is finite but the variance is
infinite, so the law of large numbers still gives convergence to the right value but without a Gaussian
error rate; if $\widehat k_i\ge 1$ even the mean is infinite and the estimate does not converge, so the
point must be evaluated by refitting. This is @thm-comp-psis-reliability.

**Why the alarm is at $0.7$ rather than $0.5$.** The theoretical variance-finiteness threshold is
$k=\tfrac12$, but for $\tfrac12\le k<1$ the estimator still converges to the correct value by the law of
large numbers, and PSIS replaces the offending upper tail of the ratios by a smooth generalized Pareto fit,
truncating and stabilizing the largest weights. Empirically this smoothing keeps the bias and variance
small enough to be usable up to about $\widehat k\approx 0.7$. The operational alarm is therefore set at the
practical $0.7$, where the smoothed estimate begins to degrade, rather than at the theoretical variance
threshold $0.5$, below which a central limit theorem holds but above which the estimate is often still
acceptable. $\square$

## Chapter 25: General Likelihoods: Survival and Ordered Categorical Outcomes

### Solution to @exr-genlik-mhr-attenuation: The marginal hazard ratio drifts away from the conditional one

This Chapter 25 exercise shows that under a mixed (frailty) population the marginal hazard ratio departs from
the constant conditional hazard ratio $\psi$ over time, because the two arms shed high-frailty individuals
from their risk sets at different rates.

**Strategy.** The marginal hazard ratio is $\psi$ times a ratio of survivor-weighted frailty means; the key
identity is that the derivative of such a tilted mean is a negative variance, which makes the mean strictly
decreasing and forces the ratio above one.

**Uses.** The time-varying marginal hazard ratio theorem @thm-marginal-hr-time-varying and the
survivor-weighted mean @eq-genlik-mhr.

A word on the survival vocabulary first. Among individuals still alive (still *at risk*) at time $s$, the
frailty distribution is no longer the population one: high-frailty individuals die faster, so the survivors
are enriched for low frailty. Because surviving to $s$ under hazard $\rho$ has probability $e^{-\rho s}$, the
*risk-set* or *survivor-weighted* mean of $\rho$ at time $s$ tilts the population law by the weight
$e^{-\rho s}$, giving $\mathbb E[\rho\mid\text{alive at }s]=\mathbb E[\rho\,e^{-\rho s}]/\mathbb E[e^{-\rho s}]$.
This tilted average is what the notation $\mathbb E_{\tilde f_a(\cdot\mid s)}[\rho]$ denotes.

Binary frailty $\rho(X)\in\{\rho_0,\rho_1\}$ with $\rho_0<\rho_1$, $P(X=1)=q$, constant baseline
$h_{a0}(s)=1$, constant conditional hazard ratio $\psi\in(0,1)$. The control survival is $S_a(s\mid x)=e^{-\rho(x)s}$
and the treated survival $S_b(s\mid x)=e^{-\psi\rho(x)s}$. By @thm-marginal-hr-time-varying,
$\mathrm{mHR}(s)=\psi\,R(s)$ with $R(s)=\mathbb E_{\tilde f_b(\cdot\mid s)}[\rho]/\mathbb E_{\tilde f_a(\cdot\mid s)}[\rho]$,
the ratio of survivor-weighted frailty means @eq-genlik-mhr.

**Closed form.** The risk-set (survivor-weighted) mean of $\rho$ under arm $a$ at time $s$ is
$g(s):=\mathbb E_{\tilde f_a(\cdot\mid s)}[\rho]=\dfrac{(1-q)\rho_0 e^{-\rho_0 s}+q\rho_1 e^{-\rho_1 s}}{(1-q)e^{-\rho_0 s}+q e^{-\rho_1 s}}$,
and under arm $b$ the survival weights are $e^{-\psi\rho(x)s}$, replacing $s$ by $\psi s$:
$\mathbb E_{\tilde f_b(\cdot\mid s)}[\rho]=g(\psi s)$. Hence
$$
R(s)=\frac{g(\psi s)}{g(s)},\qquad
g(c)=\frac{(1-q)\rho_0 e^{-\rho_0 c}+q\rho_1 e^{-\rho_1 c}}{(1-q)e^{-\rho_0 c}+q e^{-\rho_1 c}},
\qquad \mathrm{mHR}(s)=\psi\,\frac{g(\psi s)}{g(s)}.
$$

**Monotonicity of $g$ and the bound $R(s)\ge 1$.** The map $g(c)=\mathbb E[\rho\,e^{-\rho c}]/\mathbb E[e^{-\rho c}]$
is the mean of $\rho$ under the tilt $\propto e^{-\rho c}$. Its derivative is the key identity, so we derive
it. Write $N(c)=\mathbb E[\rho\,e^{-\rho c}]$ and $D(c)=\mathbb E[e^{-\rho c}]$, so $g=N/D$, and note
$N'(c)=-\mathbb E[\rho^2 e^{-\rho c}]$ and $D'(c)=-\mathbb E[\rho\,e^{-\rho c}]=-N(c)$. By the quotient rule,
$$
g'(c)=\frac{N'D-ND'}{D^2}=\frac{-\mathbb E[\rho^2 e^{-\rho c}]\,D+N^2}{D^2}
=-\frac{\mathbb E[\rho^2 e^{-\rho c}]}{D}+\Bigl(\frac{N}{D}\Bigr)^2
=-\bigl(\mathbb E_c[\rho^2]-\mathbb E_c[\rho]^2\bigr)=-\operatorname{Var}_c(\rho),
$$
where $\mathbb E_c[\cdot]$ is expectation under the tilt (so $\mathbb E_c[\rho^2]=\mathbb E[\rho^2 e^{-\rho c}]/D$
and $\mathbb E_c[\rho]=N/D$). Thus $g'(c)=-\operatorname{Var}_c(\rho)\le 0$, strictly negative for
$c\in(0,\infty)$ because $\rho$ is non-degenerate ($\rho_0\neq\rho_1$, $q\in(0,1)$). So $g$ is strictly
decreasing. Since $\psi<1$, $\psi s<s$, hence $g(\psi s)\ge g(s)$ and $R(s)\ge 1$, that is
$\mathrm{mHR}(s)\ge\psi$. At $s=0$ both tilts equal the population law, $g(0)=(1-q)\rho_0+q\rho_1$, so
$R(0)=1$; as $s\to\infty$ the risk set in both arms is dominated by the low-frailty stratum, $g(c)\to\rho_0$,
so $R(\infty)=\rho_0/\rho_0=1$. For every $s\in(0,\infty)$ the strict monotonicity gives $g(\psi s)>g(s)$,
so $R(s)>1$ and $\mathrm{mHR}(s)>\psi$. Thus $\mathrm{mHR}(s)>\psi$ on $(0,\infty)$ with
$\lim_{s\to 0^+}\mathrm{mHR}(s)=\lim_{s\to\infty}\mathrm{mHR}(s)=\psi$.

**Time of maximal attenuation.** Setting $\tfrac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm ds}R(s)=0$ gives, since
$R=g(\psi s)/g(s)$,
$$
\psi\,\frac{g'(\psi s)}{g(\psi s)}=\frac{g'(s)}{g(s)},
$$
that is, the survivor-selection rate $\mathrm d\log g/\mathrm dc=-\operatorname{Var}_c(\rho)/g(c)$,
scaled by $\psi$ in the treated arm, matches that of the control arm. At this $s$ the differential rate at
which the two arms shed high-frailty individuals from their risk sets is balanced; it is the moment of
maximal survivor selection, where the frailty composition of the two risk sets differs most and the
marginal hazard ratio departs furthest from the conditional $\psi$. With $\rho_0=1,\rho_1=3,q=\tfrac12,
\psi=\tfrac12$ this reproduces the table of @exm-genlik-survival, for instance
$\mathrm{mHR}(1)=\tfrac12\,g(0.5)/g(1)=\tfrac12(1.537883/1.238399)=0.62092$. $\square$

### Solution to @exr-genlik-rmst-transport: RMST is collapsible but not transportable

This Chapter 25 exercise shows that the restricted mean survival time (RMST) contrast is collapsible within
each population yet differs across populations with different covariate mixes, so collapsibility does not
imply transportability.

**Uses.** The RMST collapsibility theorem @thm-rmst-collapsible and conditional constancy of relative
effects on the log-hazard scale.

Two populations $\mathcal P,\mathcal P^{*}$ share the binary covariate $X$ but have prevalences $q\neq q^{*}$,
with the exponential proportional-hazards model of @exm-genlik-survival: conditional control hazard
$\lambda_x$ and treated hazard $\psi\lambda_x$, shared across populations (conditional constancy on the
log-hazard scale, with a common baseline).
The conditional RMST at horizon $\tau$ is $\operatorname{RMST}_t(\tau\mid x)=(1-e^{-\lambda_x^{(t)}\tau})/\lambda_x^{(t)}$
with $\lambda_x^{(C)}=\lambda_x$, $\lambda_x^{(A)}=\psi\lambda_x$.

**Collapsibility within a population.** By @thm-rmst-collapsible the marginal RMST contrast is the
covariate average of the conditional contrasts, $\Delta\!\operatorname{RMST}_{CA}(\tau\mid\mathcal P)=\mathbb E_{X\sim\mathcal P}[d(X)]$
with $d(x)=\operatorname{RMST}_A(\tau\mid x)-\operatorname{RMST}_C(\tau\mid x)$. For binary $X$ this is
$(1-q)d(0)+q\,d(1)$ in $\mathcal P$.

**Difference between populations.** Since the conditional contrasts $d(0),d(1)$ are the same functions in
both populations (shared hazards),
$$
\Delta\!\operatorname{RMST}_{CA}(\tau\mid\mathcal P)-\Delta\!\operatorname{RMST}_{CA}(\tau\mid\mathcal P^{*})
=\bigl[(1-q)d(0)+q\,d(1)\bigr]-\bigl[(1-q^{*})d(0)+q^{*}d(1)\bigr]
=(q-q^{*})\bigl[d(1)-d(0)\bigr].
$$
This is nonzero whenever $d(1)\neq d(0)$, that is whenever the conditional RMST contrast is modified by $X$.
It is, because RMST is a nonlinear function of the hazard: with $\lambda_0=1,\lambda_1=3,\psi=\tfrac12,\tau=2$,
$$
d(0)=\operatorname{RMST}_A(2\mid 0)-\operatorname{RMST}_C(2\mid 0)=1.2642-0.8647=0.3995,
\qquad
d(1)=0.6335-0.3325=0.3010,
$$
so $d(1)-d(0)=-0.0985$ and the two populations' RMST contrasts differ by $(q-q^{*})(-0.0985)$; for example
$q=\tfrac12,q^{*}=0.3$ gives a difference of $0.2(-0.0985)=-0.0197$ years.

**Conclusion.** RMST is collapsible (the within-population marginal equals the average conditional) yet not
transportable (the marginal differs across populations with different covariate mixes), because the shift in
the covariate distribution acts on the effect-modified conditional RMST contrast. This is unlike the
conditional log-hazard model, which is the single shared number $\log\psi$ in both populations by
assumption, hence trivially population-free. The distinction is the scale-misalignment remark following
@thm-rmst-collapsible: collapsibility is a within-population identity and does not confer the
cross-population identity of transportability, exactly the phenomenon carried into Chapter 26
(@thm-mlumr-tte). $\square$

**Common mistake (collapsibility versus transportability).** These two properties are easy to conflate but
are different guarantees. Collapsibility is a *within-population* statement: the marginal effect equals a
straight average of the conditional effects, with no Jensen gap (risk difference and RMST are collapsible;
the odds ratio and hazard ratio are not). Transportability is a *between-population* statement: the same
effect number holds in a new population with a different covariate distribution. A measure can be collapsible
yet not transportable, as RMST is here, because averaging an effect-modified conditional contrast over a
different covariate mix changes the marginal value. Do not treat "collapsible" as a license to carry a
marginal effect from a trial population to a decision population; only a conditional effect that is genuinely
constant across the relevant covariates, or an explicit standardization to the target, transports.

## Chapter 26: Multilevel Unanchored Meta-Regression

### Solution to @exr-mlumr-identify-alphaB: Identifying the comparator intercept in unanchored ML-UMR

This Chapter 26 exercise solves the two-point aggregation equation for the comparator-arm intercept
$\alpha_B$ from an observed aggregate response, then computes the conditional and marginal log odds ratios,
exhibiting the non-collapsibility gap.

**Uses.** The aggregation-equation monotonicity @lem-mlnmr-aggregate-monotone and the shared
prognostic-factor assumption (SPFA).

Logit link, SPFA prognostic slope $\beta_{\mathrm{PF}}=0.8$, single binary covariate with comparator
prevalence $\bar x_B=P(X=1)=0.4$, observed comparator response proportion $\theta_{\bullet B}^{\mathrm{obs}}=0.30$.
The two-point aggregation equation @eq-mlumr-alphaB-solve is
$$
\Theta_B(\alpha_B)=(1-0.4)\operatorname{expit}(\alpha_B)+0.4\operatorname{expit}(\alpha_B+0.8)=0.30 .
$$

**Solving by bracketing.** $\Theta_B$ is strictly increasing in $\alpha_B$ (@lem-mlnmr-aggregate-monotone),
so the root is unique. Evaluating:
$$
\Theta_B(-1.3)=0.6(0.21417)+0.4(0.37754)=0.27952,\qquad
\Theta_B(-1.2)=0.6(0.23148)+0.4(0.40131)=0.29941 .
$$
Since $\Theta_B(-1.20)<0.30<\Theta_B(-1.19)=0.30144$, linear interpolation between $-1.20$ and $-1.19$ places
the root at $\alpha_B\approx-1.20$ (to two decimals; more precisely $\alpha_B\approx-1.197$).

**Comparator-population marginal response.** By construction $\Theta_B(\alpha_B)=0.30$, so the
comparator-population marginal response under arm $B$ is $0.30$, as required.

**Log odds ratios with the index fit $\alpha_A=-0.2$.** Under SPFA the conditional log odds ratio of $A$
versus $B$ is the covariate-free constant
$$
\Delta^{\mathrm{Cond}}_{AB}=\alpha_A-\alpha_B=-0.2-(-1.197)=0.997\approx 1.00 .
$$
The comparator-population marginal response under arm $A$ is
$$
\Theta_A=(1-0.4)\operatorname{expit}(\alpha_A)+0.4\operatorname{expit}(\alpha_A+0.8)
=0.6\operatorname{expit}(-0.2)+0.4\operatorname{expit}(0.6)=0.6(0.45017)+0.4(0.64566)=0.52836,
$$
so the comparator-population marginal log odds ratio is
$$
\Delta^{\mathrm{Marg}}_{AB}=\operatorname{logit}(0.52836)-\operatorname{logit}(0.30)=0.11352-(-0.84730)=0.96082 .
$$
The marginal log odds ratio $0.96$ is smaller in magnitude than the conditional $1.00$, a non-collapsibility
gap of about $0.04$: averaging the logistic model over the comparator covariate distribution attenuates the
contrast toward the null, exactly as in the anchored ML-NMR computation. $\square$

### Solution to @exr-mlumr-rmst-transport: Population-specific RMST from an unanchored ML-UMR survival fit

This Chapter 26 exercise computes the RMST contrast at two target covariate distributions from an
exponential proportional-hazards fit, again showing the RMST contrast is collapsible within a population but
differs between populations, while the conditional log hazard ratio is a single population-free scalar.

**Uses.** The RMST collapsibility theorem @thm-rmst-collapsible and the ML-UMR time-to-event result
@thm-mlumr-tte.

For the exponential proportional-hazards survival coda, $h_k(t\mid x)=\lambda_k e^{\beta x}$ with
$\beta=\log 2$, $\lambda_A=0.10$, $\lambda_B=0.15$, so
$$
\operatorname{RMST}_k(\tau\mid x)=\frac{1-\exp(-\lambda_k e^{\beta x}\tau)}{\lambda_k e^{\beta x}}.
$$
The population RMST contrast at $P(X=1)=\pi^{*}$ is, by collapsibility (@thm-rmst-collapsible), the two-point
average
$$
\Delta\!\operatorname{RMST}_{AB}(\tau\mid\mathcal P^{*})=(1-\pi^{*})\,d(0)+\pi^{*}d(1),
\qquad d(x)=\operatorname{RMST}_A(\tau\mid x)-\operatorname{RMST}_B(\tau\mid x).
$$

**Conditional contrasts at $\tau=10$.** With $e^{\beta\cdot 0}=1$, $e^{\beta\cdot 1}=2$,
$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{RMST}_A(10\mid 0)&=\tfrac{1-e^{-1}}{0.10}=6.32121, & \operatorname{RMST}_A(10\mid 1)&=\tfrac{1-e^{-2}}{0.20}=4.32332,\\
\operatorname{RMST}_B(10\mid 0)&=\tfrac{1-e^{-1.5}}{0.15}=5.17913, & \operatorname{RMST}_B(10\mid 1)&=\tfrac{1-e^{-3}}{0.30}=3.16738,
\end{aligned}
$$
so $d(0)=6.32121-5.17913=1.14208$ and $d(1)=4.32332-3.16738=1.15594$, with $d(1)-d(0)=0.01387$.

**Collapsible but not transportable.** Within each population the marginal contrast is the average of these
conditional contrasts (collapsibility). Across populations,
$$
\Delta\!\operatorname{RMST}_{AB}(10\mid \pi^{*}=0.5)=0.5(1.14208)+0.5(1.15594)=1.14901,
\qquad
\Delta\!\operatorname{RMST}_{AB}(10\mid \pi^{*}=0.3)=0.7(1.14208)+0.3(1.15594)=1.14624,
$$
which differ by $(0.5-0.3)(d(1)-d(0))=0.2(0.01387)=0.00277$ years. So the RMST contrast is collapsible
within each population yet differs between the two populations: collapsibility does not imply
transportability. By contrast the conditional log hazard ratio of $A$ versus $B$ is the single number
$\log(\lambda_A/\lambda_B)=\log(0.10/0.15)=-\log 1.5$ in every population, covariate-free and time-invariant.
This is @thm-mlumr-tte(e): an unanchored ML-UMR analysis can report the population-specific RMST contrast at
any target $\pi^{*}$, but only the conditional log hazard ratio is a single population-free scalar. $\square$

## Chapter 27: Aggregate-Level Covariate-Distance Matching

### Solution to @exr-distance-affine-invariance: Mahalanobis distance is affine-invariant, Euclidean is not

This Chapter 27 exercise proves the Mahalanobis distance between covariate means is unchanged by any
invertible affine reparameterization of the covariates, whereas the standardized Euclidean distance can even
reverse rankings, because it discards the off-diagonal covariance.

**Uses.** The Mahalanobis distance definition @def-mahalanobis-distance and the whitening interpretation
(Mahalanobis is Euclidean distance after standardizing by the covariance).

Let the covariates be reparameterized by an invertible affine map $\mathbf x\mapsto A\mathbf x+\mathbf c$,
with the covariance transformed accordingly to $A\boldsymbol\Sigma A^\top$. A gap between two means
$\boldsymbol\delta=\bar{\mathbf x}_j-\bar{\mathbf x}_0$ transforms to $A\boldsymbol\delta$ (the constant
$\mathbf c$ cancels in the difference). The Mahalanobis distance (@def-mahalanobis-distance) becomes
$$
d_M^2=(A\boldsymbol\delta)^\top(A\boldsymbol\Sigma A^\top)^{-1}(A\boldsymbol\delta)
=\boldsymbol\delta^\top A^\top A^{-\top}\boldsymbol\Sigma^{-1}A^{-1}A\boldsymbol\delta
=\boldsymbol\delta^\top\boldsymbol\Sigma^{-1}\boldsymbol\delta,
$$
using $(A\boldsymbol\Sigma A^\top)^{-1}=A^{-\top}\boldsymbol\Sigma^{-1}A^{-1}$ and $A^\top A^{-\top}=I$,
$A^{-1}A=I$. So the Mahalanobis distance is unchanged under every invertible affine reparameterization. The
standardized Euclidean distance uses only the diagonal of $\boldsymbol\Sigma$ as scales; under
$\mathbf x\mapsto A\mathbf x+\mathbf c$ the scales become the diagonal of $A\boldsymbol\Sigma A^\top$, which
for a nondiagonal $A$ mixes the coordinates and is not the coordinatewise rescaling of the original scales.
For diagonal $A=\operatorname{diag}(a_1,\dots,a_p)$ each coordinate is scaled by $a_\ell$ and its standard
deviation by $|a_\ell|$, so the ratio $\delta_\ell/s_\ell$ is unchanged in magnitude and the standardized
Euclidean distance is invariant; for nondiagonal $A$ it generally is not.

**A reversing example.** Work in $\mathbb R^2$ with original covariance $\boldsymbol\Sigma=I$, so initially
Mahalanobis and standardized Euclidean both equal ordinary Euclidean distance. Take the two candidate gaps
$\boldsymbol\delta_a=(1.4,0)$ and $\boldsymbol\delta_b=(0,1)$, so Mahalanobis ranks $a$ as the more distant
($1.4>1$). Apply the nondiagonal shear $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$, giving
$\boldsymbol\delta_a'=A\boldsymbol\delta_a=(1.4,0)$, $\boldsymbol\delta_b'=A\boldsymbol\delta_b=(1,1)$, and
covariance $\boldsymbol\Sigma'=AA^\top=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$ with
$(\boldsymbol\Sigma')^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\-1&2\end{pmatrix}$. The Mahalanobis distances are preserved,
$d_M(\boldsymbol\delta_a')^2=(1.4,0)(\boldsymbol\Sigma')^{-1}(1.4,0)^\top=1.96$ and
$d_M(\boldsymbol\delta_b')^2=(1,1)(\boldsymbol\Sigma')^{-1}(1,1)^\top=1$, so $a$ remains more distant
($1.4>1$). But the standardized Euclidean distance now uses the new scales
$\operatorname{diag}(\boldsymbol\Sigma')=(2,1)$:
$$
d_{SE}(\boldsymbol\delta_a')^2=\frac{1.4^2}{2}+\frac{0^2}{1}=0.98,
\qquad
d_{SE}(\boldsymbol\delta_b')^2=\frac{1^2}{2}+\frac{1^2}{1}=1.5,
$$
so the standardized Euclidean ranking is reversed: it now calls $b$ the more distant candidate
($\sqrt{1.5}>\sqrt{0.98}$), whereas before the reparameterization it agreed with Mahalanobis that $a$ was
farther. The Mahalanobis ranking is preserved throughout. This is the precise sense in which Mahalanobis
distance is the coordinate-free member of the family: it depends only on the geometry of the covariate cloud
(it is the Euclidean distance after whitening), so any invertible affine relabeling leaves it and its
rankings intact, while standardized Euclidean distance, which discards the off-diagonal covariance, is tied
to the chosen coordinates. $\square$

### Solution to @exr-distance-secondmoment: A small moment distance does not certify an unbiased comparison

This Chapter 27 exercise builds two covariate distributions with identical first and second moments but
different target effects under a nonlinear (quartic) contrast, showing that matching a finite set of moments
leaves a residual bias for contrasts whose curvature reaches beyond those moments.

**Uses.** The diagnostic-not-validity proposition @prp-distance-diagnostic-not-validity and the second-moment
MAIC balancing of Chapter 18.

Construct two scalar covariate distributions with identical first and second moments but different target
effects under a nonlinear contrast, strengthening @prp-distance-diagnostic-not-validity. Let
$\mathcal P_0$ put mass $\tfrac12$ at each of $\pm 1$, and $\mathcal P_1$ put mass $\tfrac34$ at $0$ and
mass $\tfrac18$ at each of $\pm 2$.

**Equal first two moments.** Both are symmetric about $0$, so each has mean $0$. Their variances are
$$
\operatorname{Var}_{\mathcal P_0}=\tfrac12(1)+\tfrac12(1)=1,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}_{\mathcal P_1}=\tfrac34(0)+\tfrac18(4)+\tfrac18(4)=1 .
$$
So any diagnostic built from the first two moments (mean and variance, hence standardized Euclidean or
Mahalanobis distance between the two distributions' moment summaries) reports zero distance.

**Different target effect under a quartic contrast.** Take $\tau(x)=x^4$. The target effects are
$$
\mathbb E_{\mathcal P_0}[\tau(X)]=\tfrac12(1)+\tfrac12(1)=1,
\qquad
\mathbb E_{\mathcal P_1}[\tau(X)]=\tfrac34(0)+\tfrac18(16)+\tfrac18(16)=4 .
$$
The two target effects are $1$ and $4$, so the bias from treating the two populations as exchangeable under
this contrast is $4-1=3$, despite zero distance under any first-two-moment diagnostic.

**Implication for MAIC second-moment balancing.** Matching through any fixed finite set of moments controls
only the corresponding low-order features of the covariate distribution. A sufficiently nonlinear contrast
(here a quartic, sensitive to the fourth moment) responds to features the matched moments do not constrain,
leaving a residual bias. Balancing means and variances is therefore not enough in general: MAIC weights that
equate the first two moments still leave a target-effect discrepancy for contrasts whose curvature reaches
beyond those moments, which is why a small moment distance is a diagnostic of similarity, not a certificate
of validity. Concretely, a regulator reviewing a submitted MAIC should not accept a small Mahalanobis
distance, or a report that "all covariate means and variances are balanced," as evidence that the indirect
comparison is unbiased. The example above has zero first-two-moment distance yet a target-effect bias of
$3$; the missing ingredient is the shape of the outcome-covariate relationship, which no fixed number of
matched moments can guarantee. The right posture is to treat moment balance as necessary housekeeping and to
argue separately, from subject-matter knowledge, that the outcome model is not so nonlinear in the unbalanced
higher moments that a residual bias survives. $\square$

## Chapter 28: Quantitative Bias Analysis for Indirect Comparisons

### Solution to @exr-qba-itc-evalue-star: The E-value for an indirect comparison, and when it is infinite

This Chapter 28 exercise recomputes the sensitivity curve and E-value for an indirect comparison under a
stronger unreported covariate, and shows when the infinite value, a certificate that no single-covariate
imbalance can explain away the observed effect, is and is not available.

**Strategy.** The adjusted effect is linear in the unreported covariate's mean, $\Delta(m)=K+\beta_U m$; the
whole analysis rests on the constant $K$, which is a Gaussian-MGF integral of the log-linear model. Derive
$K$ once, then read the bias factor and E-value off the standard formulas.

**Uses.** The indirect-comparison E-value proposition @prp-itc-evalue and the lognormal (Gaussian
moment-generating-function) mean of a log-linear model.

**(a) Recomputed constants.** First, where $K$ comes from. The worked-example model is log-linear,
$\log\mu(R,U)=\beta_0+\beta_R R+\beta_U U$, with independent Gaussian covariates $R\sim\mathcal N(m_R,\sigma_R^2)$
and $U\sim\mathcal N(m,\sigma_U^2)$. Taking the marginal mean by the Gaussian moment generating function
($\mathbb E[e^{tZ}]=e^{tm_Z+t^2\sigma_Z^2/2}$ for $Z\sim\mathcal N(m_Z,\sigma_Z^2)$),
$$
\log\mathbb E[Y]=\beta_0+\beta_R m_R+\tfrac12\beta_R^2\sigma_R^2+\beta_U m+\tfrac12\beta_U^2\sigma_U^2 .
$$
The adjusted effect $\Delta(m)$ is this marginal log-mean minus the observed baseline $\log\mu_0$, so
grouping every term that does not involve $m$ into a single constant,
$$
\Delta(m)=\underbrace{\bigl(\beta_0+\beta_R m_R+\tfrac12\beta_R^2\sigma_R^2+\tfrac12\beta_U^2\sigma_U^2-\log\mu_0\bigr)}_{K}+\beta_U m,
$$
which is the sensitivity curve and defines $K$. Now use $\beta_0=-1.0$, $\beta_R=0.4$, $m_R=1.0$,
$\sigma_R=0.5$, $\sigma_U=1.0$, $\mu_0=0.47$, $\bar x_U=2.0$, but now a stronger unreported covariate
$\beta_U=-0.8$:
$$
K=\beta_0+\beta_R m_R+\tfrac12\beta_R^2\sigma_R^2+\tfrac12\beta_U^2\sigma_U^2-\log\mu_0
=-1.0+0.4+\tfrac12(0.16)(0.25)+\tfrac12(0.64)(1)-\log(0.47),
$$
that is $K=-1.0+0.4+0.02+0.32+0.75502=0.49502$. The sensitivity curve is
$\Delta(m)=K+\beta_U m=0.49502-0.8m$, so the adjusted effect at the IPD value is
$\Delta(2.0)=0.49502-1.6=-1.10498$. The observed bias factor is
$\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}}=\exp(|\Delta(2.0)|)=\exp(1.10498)=3.0192$, and the per-liter risk ratio is
$\exp(|\beta_U|)=\exp(0.8)=2.2255$.

**(b) The E-value.** The per-liter risk ratio $2.2255$ is below $\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}}=3.0192$, so
reading it as $\mathrm{RR}_{UD}$ would place us in the third case of @def-itc-evalue and declare
$E_{\mathrm{ITC}}=+\infty$. That certificate would be false: the sensitivity curve crosses the null at
$m^{\dagger}=K/|\beta_U|=0.49502/0.8=0.619$ liters, so a comparator mean $1.38$ liters below the IPD value
reverses the conclusion. In @eq-qba-sensitivity-params, $\mathrm{RR}_{UD}$ is the ratio of risks between the
*extreme* levels of $U$; for continuous, unbounded $\mathrm{FEV}_1$ it is $+\infty$, and @eq-qba-itc-evalue
gives $E_{\mathrm{ITC}}=\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}}=3.0192$, the $y\to\infty$ limit of
@cor-itc-evalue-monotone. The certificate is available only for a binary or bounded covariate. As a
check of the finite formula on the artificial pair $\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}}=1.5$, $\mathrm{RR}_{UD}=2.5$
(where $1<1.5<2.5$),
$$
E_{\mathrm{ITC}}=\frac{\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}}(\mathrm{RR}_{UD}-1)}{\mathrm{RR}_{UD}-\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}}}
=\frac{1.5(2.5-1)}{2.5-1.5}=\frac{2.25}{1}=2.25 .
$$

**(c) The certificate.** For fixed $\mathrm{RR}_{UD}=y>1$, the bias factor
$\mathrm{BF}_U(x,y)=\dfrac{xy}{x+y-1}=\dfrac{y}{1+(y-1)/x}$ as a function of $x=\mathrm{RR}_{EU}$ has
derivative
$$
\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\frac{xy}{x+y-1}=\frac{y(x+y-1)-xy}{(x+y-1)^2}=\frac{y(y-1)}{(x+y-1)^2}>0,
$$
so it is strictly increasing in $x$. Moreover $1+(y-1)/x>1$ for all finite $x>0$, so
$\mathrm{BF}_U(x,y)<y=\mathrm{RR}_{UD}$, and as $x\to\infty$, $(y-1)/x\to 0$ and
$\mathrm{BF}_U(x,y)\uparrow y$. Hence the bias factor is strictly increasing in $\mathrm{RR}_{EU}$ and
bounded above by $\mathrm{RR}_{UD}$, the bound approached but never attained. Consequently, when
$\mathrm{RR}_{UD}\le\mathrm{BF}_{\mathrm{obs}}$, the target is unreachable for every finite imbalance and the
result cannot be explained away by imbalance of this one covariate, which is the meaning of
$E_{\mathrm{ITC}}=+\infty$. $\square$

### Solution to @exr-qba-norta-margins-star: NORTA marginal recovery, copula non-uniqueness, and Pearson drift

This Chapter 28 exercise checks three facts about the NORTA (normal-to-anything) construction: (a) it
recovers a discrete Bernoulli margin exactly, (b) for discrete margins the copula is not uniquely determined
by the joint law (Sklar non-uniqueness), and (c) for continuous margins the covariate Pearson correlation
need not equal the latent normal correlation.

**Strategy.** Separate the two questions the exercise mixes together: marginal recovery uses only that
$\Phi(Z)$ is uniform, while the dependence questions are about the copula. Keep the identification of the
Gaussian parameter distinct from the Sklar non-uniqueness of the copula function.

**Uses.** The NORTA/Gaussian-copula theorem @thm-norta-copula and the Gaussian moment generating function.

Some copula vocabulary, since the exercise leans on it. The *Frechet (Frechet-Hoeffding) bounds* say every
joint distribution with given margins lies between two extremes: the *countermonotone* coupling (perfect
negative dependence, each variable a decreasing function of the other) below and the *comonotone* coupling
(perfect positive dependence) above. *Sklar's theorem* guarantees a copula $C$ with $F(x_1,x_2)=C(F_1(x_1),F_2(x_2))$;
this $C$ is unique on the set $\operatorname{Range}(F_1)\times\operatorname{Range}(F_2)$, which is all of
$[0,1]^2$ for continuous margins (so $C$ is unique) but only a coarse grid for discrete margins (so $C$ is
free between grid points). That grid-only determination is the *Sklar non-uniqueness* of part (b).

Let $F$ be the $\mathrm{Ber}(\pi)$ distribution function and $Z\sim\mathcal N(0,1)$.

**(a) Discrete margin recovery.** The generalized inverse of the Bernoulli distribution function is
$$
F^{-1}(u)=\inf\{x:F(x)\ge u\}=\begin{cases}0,& 0<u\le 1-\pi,\\ 1,& 1-\pi<u\le 1.\end{cases}
$$
Since $\Phi(Z)\sim\mathrm{Unif}(0,1)$ (the probability integral transform), $X=F^{-1}(\Phi(Z))$ equals $1$
exactly when $\Phi(Z)>1-\pi$, an event of probability $1-(1-\pi)=\pi$, and equals $0$ otherwise. Hence
$X\sim\mathrm{Ber}(\pi)$, confirming @thm-norta-copula(1) for a discrete margin, with no continuity needed.

**(b) Non-uniqueness of the copula for discrete margins.** It is important to separate two claims that are
easy to run together. Take two such Bernoulli variables $X_1=F^{-1}(\Phi(Z_1))$, $X_2=F^{-1}(\Phi(Z_2))$
with $(Z_1,Z_2)$ bivariate normal of correlation $\rho^N$. The joint law of $(X_1,X_2)$ is determined by the
single cell probability
$$
P(X_1=1,X_2=1)=P\bigl(\Phi(Z_1)>1-\pi,\ \Phi(Z_2)>1-\pi\bigr)=P(Z_1>z_\pi,Z_2>z_\pi),\qquad z_\pi=\Phi^{-1}(1-\pi),
$$
which is a continuous, strictly increasing function of $\rho^N$ on $[-1,1]$ for fixed $\pi\in(0,1)$.

*First claim (the Gaussian parameter is identified).* Because this cell probability is strictly increasing
in $\rho^N$, it is injective: distinct latent correlations $\rho^N$ give distinct cell probabilities and
hence distinct bivariate Bernoulli laws. So within the Gaussian (NORTA) family the parameter $\rho^N$ is
recovered from the joint law; there is no ambiguity of the Gaussian parameter in the nondegenerate case.

*Second claim (the copula function is not unique).* The non-uniqueness the exercise is after is a different,
Sklar-level statement, and it is not about $\rho^N$ at all. Sklar's theorem determines the copula only on
$\operatorname{Range}(F_1)\times\operatorname{Range}(F_2)$; for a Bernoulli margin that range is the finite
set $\{0,\,1-\pi,\,1\}$, so the copula $C$ is pinned only at those grid points and is free to be interpolated
in infinitely many ways between them. Many distinct copula functions, most of them not Gaussian at all,
reproduce the same bivariate Bernoulli law, because a discrete margin can only "see" the copula on its coarse
grid. That is the sense in which the copula is non-unique for discrete margins: not that two Gaussian
parameters collide, but that the copula function is underdetermined once the margins are discrete. The range
of attainable cell probabilities is itself limited by the Frechet bounds, with the comonotone and
countermonotone couplings as the extremes; a target joint law outside that attainable interval has no
Gaussian $\rho^N$ realizing it. Marginal recovery in (a), by contrast, holds for every $\rho^N$, because it
used only that $\Phi(Z_j)$ is uniform, irrespective of the dependence.

**(c) Pearson correlation need not equal $\rho^N$ for continuous margins.** Take $F_1=F_2$ a lognormal
margin, $X_j=\exp(\sigma Z_j)$ with $(Z_1,Z_2)$ standard bivariate normal of correlation $\rho^N$. The
degenerate value $\rho^N=1$ is not informative here: then $Z_1=Z_2$, so $X_1=X_2$ and trivially
$\operatorname{corr}(X_1,X_2)=1=\rho^N$, which cannot exhibit strict inequality. So take a genuinely
dependent case, $\rho^N\in(-1,1)$, and compute the covariate Pearson correlation in closed form from the
Gaussian moment generating function. With $\mathbb E[e^{tZ}]=e^{t^2/2}$ for a standard normal and
$Z_1+Z_2\sim\mathcal N(0,\,2+2\rho^N)$,
$$
\mathbb E[X_j]=e^{\sigma^2/2},\qquad \mathbb E[X_j^2]=e^{2\sigma^2},\qquad
\mathbb E[X_1X_2]=\mathbb E\bigl[e^{\sigma(Z_1+Z_2)}\bigr]=e^{\sigma^2(1+\rho^N)} .
$$
Hence $\operatorname{Var}(X_j)=e^{2\sigma^2}-e^{\sigma^2}=e^{\sigma^2}(e^{\sigma^2}-1)$ and
$\operatorname{Cov}(X_1,X_2)=e^{\sigma^2(1+\rho^N)}-e^{\sigma^2}=e^{\sigma^2}(e^{\sigma^2\rho^N}-1)$, so the
$e^{\sigma^2}$ factors cancel and
$$
\operatorname{corr}(X_1,X_2)=\frac{e^{\sigma^2\rho^N}-1}{e^{\sigma^2}-1} .
$$
For $\sigma=1$ and $\rho^N=0.5$ this is $(e^{0.5}-1)/(e-1)=0.64872/1.71828=0.37752\neq 0.5$. The Pearson
correlation of the lognormal covariates ($0.3775$) differs from the latent normal correlation ($0.5$),
because the nonlinear exponential margin reshapes the dependence; only the rank correlation is preserved.
This is exactly why $\boldsymbol\Omega$ in the NORTA and Gaussian-copula construction is the correlation of
the latent normals, not of the covariates. $\square$

## Chapter 29: Simulation Study Theory

### Solution to @exr-sim-power: Sample size, power, and the test-interval duality

This Chapter 29 exercise computes the standardized signal and the sample size for a target power, checks
that the wrong-side rejection term is negligible, and shows the power calculation and the
confidence-interval-width calculation are two readings of the same inequality.

**Uses.** The simulation power formula @thm-sim-power and its exact two-term version @eq-sim-power.

A study targets a true contrast $\theta=0.4$ against $\theta_0=0$ at level $\alpha=0.05$, with standard
error $\sigma_n=c/\sqrt n$, $c=2.0$.

**(a) Standardized signal.** By @thm-sim-power the standardized signal is
$$
\Delta_n=\frac{\theta-\theta_0}{\sigma_n}=\frac{0.4}{2.0/\sqrt n}=\frac{0.4}{2.0}\sqrt n=0.2\sqrt n .
$$

**(b) Sample size for power $0.80$.** Using the one-sided approximation
$\mathrm{Power}\approx\Phi(\Delta_n-z_{\alpha/2})$ with $z_{\alpha/2}=z_{0.025}=1.95996$ and
$\Phi^{-1}(0.80)=0.84162$, set $\Delta_n-1.95996=0.84162$, so $\Delta_n=2.80158$. Then
$0.2\sqrt n=2.80158$, $\sqrt n=14.0079$, and $n=196.2$, rounded up to $n=197$.

**(c) The dropped term is negligible.** The exact two-term power @eq-sim-power is
$\Phi(\Delta_n-z_{\alpha/2})+\Phi(-\Delta_n-z_{\alpha/2})$. At $\Delta_n=2.80158$ the dropped term is
$$
\Phi(-\Delta_n-z_{\alpha/2})=\Phi(-2.80158-1.95996)=\Phi(-4.7615)\approx 9.6\times 10^{-7},
$$
below one part in a million, so the one-term and two-term power formulas agree to far more than the
precision of any simulation; the second term is the probability of rejecting on the wrong side and is
negligible for a signal this large.

**(d) Test-interval duality.** The Wald test rejects $\theta_0$ exactly when $\theta_0$ lies outside the
interval $\hat\theta_n\pm z_{\alpha/2}\sigma_n$. Power $0.80$ to reject $\theta_0=0$ when the truth is
$\theta=0.4$ is therefore the probability $0.80$ that the $95\%$ confidence interval of half-width
$z_{\alpha/2}\sigma_n$ excludes $0$, which holds when $|\theta-\theta_0|\ge(z_{\alpha/2}+z_{0.20})\sigma_n$,
the same standardized-signal condition $\Delta_n\ge z_{\alpha/2}+\Phi^{-1}(0.80)$ and hence the same $n$.
The power calculation and the confidence-interval-width calculation are two readings of one inequality.
$\square$

### Solution to @exr-sim-bias-variance-tradeoff: When balancing fewer covariates lowers mean squared error

This Chapter 29 exercise sets up the bias-variance trade-off of covariate balancing: dropping a covariate
saves effective sample size (variance) at the cost of some bias, and balancing the smaller set wins on mean
squared error exactly when that bias is below a variance-set threshold.

**Uses.** The bias-variance (mean-squared-error) decomposition @thm-mse-decomposition and the MAIC effective
sample-size bound @thm-maic-ess-bound.

In the geometry of @exm-sim-miniature, compare two adjusted estimators: balancing only the effect modifier
$x_1$ leaves a small omitted-covariate bias $\beta$ on a non-collapsible scale but retains effective sample
size $\mathrm{ESS}_1$, with variance $\sigma^2 n/\mathrm{ESS}_1$; balancing both $x_1$ and the prognostic
$x_2$ removes the bias but lowers the effective sample size to $\mathrm{ESS}_2<\mathrm{ESS}_1$, with variance
$\sigma^2 n/\mathrm{ESS}_2$.

**(a) Mean squared errors.** By the bias-variance decomposition @thm-mse-decomposition,
$\mathrm{MSE}=\mathrm{bias}^2+\mathrm{variance}$:
$$
\mathrm{MSE}_1=\beta^2+\frac{\sigma^2 n}{\mathrm{ESS}_1},
\qquad
\mathrm{MSE}_2=0+\frac{\sigma^2 n}{\mathrm{ESS}_2}.
$$

**(b) When balancing only $x_1$ wins.** $\mathrm{MSE}_1<\mathrm{MSE}_2$ if and only if
$$
\beta^2+\frac{\sigma^2 n}{\mathrm{ESS}_1}<\frac{\sigma^2 n}{\mathrm{ESS}_2},
\qquad\text{that is}\qquad
\beta^2<\sigma^2 n\Bigl(\frac{1}{\mathrm{ESS}_2}-\frac{1}{\mathrm{ESS}_1}\Bigr)
=\sigma^2 n\,\frac{\mathrm{ESS}_1-\mathrm{ESS}_2}{\mathrm{ESS}_1\,\mathrm{ESS}_2}.
$$
Equivalently $|\beta|<\sigma\sqrt{n(\mathrm{ESS}_1-\mathrm{ESS}_2)/(\mathrm{ESS}_1\mathrm{ESS}_2)}$: the
smaller-set estimator achieves the lower mean squared error exactly when its bias is below the threshold set
by the variance saved through the larger effective sample size.

**(c) Relation to ESS and the identity scale.** Balancing the additional covariate $x_2$ adds a moment
constraint to the weights, which typically lowers the effective sample size (the exercise assumes
$\mathrm{ESS}_2<\mathrm{ESS}_1$; @thm-maic-ess-bound caps both at $n$), raising the variance; this is the variance cost on the right-hand side of
the condition. The trade-off in (b) is the bias-variance balance of the remark following
@lem-sim-mse-empirical-identity: balancing a covariate is worthwhile only when the bias it removes exceeds
the variance it costs. On the identity scale a purely prognostic covariate carries no bias, $\beta=0$,
because it cancels in the contrast (it shifts both arms equally); then the condition $\beta^2=0<\sigma^2 n(\cdots)$
holds automatically, so balancing $x_2$ removes no bias while lowering the effective sample size,
and it can only hurt. $\square$

## Chapter 30: Machine-Checked Foundations: The Coq Formalization

### Solution to @exr-coq-discrete-vs-named: Why one Coq theorem needs no premise and another carries one

This Chapter 30 exercise contrasts two machine-checked results and explains why the discrete balancing
theorem is proved outright while the continuous inverse-probability-weighting identity must carry a named,
unproved premise.

**A reminder on the tiers (for readers who jumped straight here).** The formalization sorts theorems by how
much they assume. A *tier F* ("fully proved") theorem is proved from first principles inside Coq with no
unproved input. A *tier P* ("proved given a premise") theorem is a complete Coq proof of an implication
whose hypothesis is a *named premise*: an abstract, explicitly stated proposition that the current libraries
cannot yet discharge, made visible in the theorem's own statement rather than hidden. Schematically the two
shapes are

```coq
(* tier F: proved outright, no probabilistic hypothesis *)
Theorem propensity_score_is_balancing :
  forall x, balancing_property x.

(* tier P: a complete proof of an implication whose premise Hipw1 is stated, not proved *)
Theorem mu1_IPW_unbiased :
  Hipw1 -> estimator_IPW = mu1_true.
```

The point of the exercise is to explain why the first needs nothing to the left of its conclusion while the
second must display `Hipw1`.

Contrast `propensity_score_is_balancing`, a tier-**F** result with no probabilistic premise, against
`mu1_IPW_unbiased`, a tier-**P** result carrying the named premise `Hipw1`.

**Why the discrete balancing theorem needs no premise.** The Rosenbaum-Rubin balancing property is proved
over a finite discrete model, a joint probability mass function over finite types, with conditional
independence written in the cross-multiplied form @eq-coq-dci,
$q_{XYZ}(x,y,z)\,q_Z(z)=q_{XZ}(x,z)\,q_{YZ}(y,z)$. In this multiplicative form the statement needs no
positivity hypothesis: when a conditioning mass is zero, both sides vanish by marginal monotonicity (every
joint marginal is dominated by the conditioning mass), so the identity holds trivially at zero-mass
covariate points rather than requiring a nonzero denominator. There is therefore no division to justify and
no probabilistic fact to admit; the proof goes through outright in Coq for every covariate value, including
those of measure zero, and the theorem is tier **F**.

**Why the continuous IPW identity defers to `Hipw1`.** The inverse-probability-weighting unbiasedness
`mu1_IPW_unbiased` is a statement in the continuous kernel model, and its proof needs the tower property
(law of total expectation) for conditional expectations under a continuous covariate law. As
@sec-coq-boundary explains, the development is built on mathcomp-analysis, which does not yet supply the
conditional-expectation and disintegration library needed to discharge that step inside Coq. So rather than
hide the gap, the tower-property consequence is admitted as the visible named premise `Hipw1`, and the
theorem is tier **P**: a fully proved Coq object given `Hipw1`, but resting on a stated, unproved
probabilistic input.

**What would close the gap, and where the paper proof lives.** Discharging `Hipw1` inside Coq requires
developing, on top of mathcomp-analysis, a measure-theoretic conditional-expectation theory with the tower
property and a disintegration (regular conditional distribution) library for the kernel model. Until that
exists, the paper proof of the premise is supplied by the potential-outcomes and adjustment chapters: the
IPW unbiasedness identity is proved there (@thm-ipw-unbiased in Chapter 10, resting on the identification
results of Chapter 9), which is exactly the tower-property argument that `Hipw1` abbreviates. $\square$

### Solution to @exr-coq-faithfulness: The placeholder trap and statement faithfulness

This Chapter 30 exercise shows how a formalization can type-check yet certify nothing, if a modeling
assumption is replaced by the trivially true proposition, and explains the structural policy that guards
against it.

**Uses.** The statement-faithfulness guarantee @sec-coq-guarantees and the visible-premise policy
@sec-coq-boundary.

Suppose a developer had defined a modeling assumption as the trivially true proposition,
`Definition conditional_constancy : Prop := True`, instead of as an abstract named proposition with real
content.

**The placeholder trap.** A "consistency theorem" of the shape
`conditional_constancy -> (estimator = truth)` then unfolds to `True -> (estimator = truth)`, which is
logically equivalent to `estimator = truth`. If, as is typical of a placeholder development, the
`estimator` and `truth` terms are wired to be definitionally or provably equal (for instance both reduce to
the same standardized integral), the implication is discharged by `intros; reflexivity` with no
mathematical content: the premise contributes nothing because every proof of `True` is vacuous, and the
conclusion was already provable on its own. The theorem type-checks and the kernel certifies it, yet it
certifies nothing about the substantive assumption its name advertises.

**Which guarantee is violated.** This is precisely the *statement faithfulness* gap of
@sec-coq-guarantees: the kernel checks that the proof proves the stated theorem, but it cannot check that
the stated theorem is the one the mathematician meant. A formalization with an unintended hypothesis that
renders the proposition vacuous type-checks just as readily as the intended one. Replacing a real modeling
restriction by `True` substitutes a vacuous proposition for the intended conditional-constancy assumption,
so the certified statement is no longer a faithful formalization of "under conditional constancy, the
estimator is consistent," even though it compiles.

**The structural defense.** The development's stated policy, recorded in `MAIC.v` and `STC.v`, is to refuse
`True`-valued assumption definitions and instead make every modeling assumption a visible, abstract named
premise that appears in the theorem's own statement (@sec-coq-boundary). Because such a premise is an
opaque `Prop`, it cannot be unfolded to `True`: whatever the proof takes from it must come through its
stated content, and a human reading the statement can confirm that the premise says what the book says. Making each assumption a load-bearing visible premise is the
structural guard against the placeholder trap, since it converts the unprovable question "is this the
intended theorem?" into the checkable question "is this premise the intended assumption?", which a reader
can answer by inspection. $\square$
